questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client's ability to reach across midline and shake hands as part of a mobility assessment. The client is unable to perform this task. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Assign Level 1 (maximum assist) mobility
Instruct the client to march in place
Apply a gait belt and ambulate the client
Document the client as Level 4, no assist

questions.explanation: A client who cannot perform the Level 1 handshake/sitting tasks is assigned maximum assist per the BMAT, requiring a mechanical lift and 2 or more staff before any further mobility attempts.

questions.prompt: A charge nurse is teaching a nursing student about the role of proprioception in maintaining balance. Which statement should the charge nurse include?

options.text: It's the sensory feedback from muscles and joints that creates the brain's awareness of body position.
It's the process bones use to produce red blood cells.
It's the hardening of bone tissue that occurs with age.
It's the chemical signal muscles send to relax after contracting.

questions.explanation: Proprioception (kinesthesia) is sensory feedback from muscles and joints that creates self-awareness of body position, enabling balance and coordination.

questions.prompt: A charge nurse is teaching a nursing student about the difference between tendons and ligaments. Which statement by the student indicates understanding?

options.text: Tendons connect muscles to bones, and ligaments connect bone to bone.
Tendons and ligaments both connect muscle to muscle.
Ligaments produce the force that moves bones.
Tendons cushion joints so the bones don't rub together.

questions.explanation: Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone. Cartilage, not tendons, cushions joints.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about the role of the skeletal system beyond movement. Which statement by the student indicates understanding?

options.text: Bones store calcium and produce blood cells in addition to supporting the body.
Bones only provide a framework for movement.
Bones do not play a role in protecting organs.
Bone marrow has no function related to blood cells.

questions.explanation: In addition to support and movement, bones protect organs, produce blood cells in the marrow, and store minerals like calcium.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to reposition a client who is unable to assist. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Obtain assistance from another staff member
Bend at the waist to grasp the draw sheet
Reposition the client without raising the bed
Twist at the torso to pull the client up in bed

questions.explanation: Getting lift assistance before moving a client who cannot assist decreases injury risk to both nurse and client, and should happen before repositioning begins.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing assistants about proper body mechanics when lifting. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bend your knees, not your back.
options.rationale: Bending the knees lowers the center of gravity and lets the leg muscles do the work.

options.text: Keep the object as far from your body as possible.
options.rationale: Holding a load away from the body increases strain on the back; keep it close.

options.text: Pivot your feet instead of twisting your torso.
options.rationale: Pivoting avoids twisting the spine, which can injure the back.

options.text: Keep your feet close together to stay steady.
options.rationale: Feet should be shoulder-width apart; a wider base of support is more stable.

options.text: Lift using the muscles in your lower back.
options.rationale: The lower back muscles are prone to injury; the leg muscles should do the lifting.

questions.explanation: Bending the knees and pivoting instead of twisting are correct body mechanics. Feet should be shoulder-width apart for a wide base, objects should stay close to the body, and lifting should use the leg muscles, not the back.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client's caregiver about ergonomics in the home. Which statement by the caregiver indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: I'll keep frequently used items on a shelf that's easy to reach without bending.
I'll try to lift my spouse alone to save time between tasks.
I'll use a shower chair to make bathing safer.
I'll make sure the walking path is clear of clutter.

questions.explanation: Solo lifting increases injury risk; 'minimal lift' or 'never lift alone' practices are core ergonomic safety principles, so this statement shows a need for further teaching.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client on prolonged bed rest who reports sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and a rapid pulse. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the provider immediately
Encourage the client to use an incentive spirometer
Apply antiembolic stockings
Document the findings and reassess in 1 hour

questions.explanation: These are manifestations of a pulmonary embolism, a life-threatening complication of immobility, requiring immediate provider notification.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about disuse osteoporosis. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: Bed rest reduces the mechanical stress your bones need to stay strong.
Bed rest increases the rate new bone is made.
Disuse osteoporosis only affects the spine.
Osteoporosis from bed rest rebuilds faster than muscle loss.

questions.explanation: Prolonged immobility reduces mechanical load on bones, disrupting the normal balance between bone growth and breakdown, leading to demineralization. Rebuilding bone mass takes longer than rebuilding muscle.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about signs of a possible deep vein thrombosis. Which statements by the client indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: I should watch for swelling, warmth, or redness in one leg.
I should massage the area if it feels tender.
I should tell the nurse if one calf looks bigger than the other.
I can cross my legs to relieve pressure.
I should tell the nurse about any new leg pain.

questions.explanation: Swelling, warmth, redness, a unilateral calf size difference, and new leg pain are all DVT manifestations. Massaging a suspected clot or crossing the legs, which compresses veins, are unsafe.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to ambulate a client for the first time since surgery. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Have the client sit on the edge of the bed for a few minutes before standing
Assist the client to stand and start walking immediately
Remove the client's nonskid footwear for comfort
Instruct the client to hold their breath while standing

questions.explanation: Sitting briefly before standing allows the nurse to assess for orthostatic hypotension before full ambulation, reducing fall risk.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has a left leg injury how to use a cane. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll hold the cane in my right hand.
I'll hold the cane in my left hand.
I'll move my right leg forward first, then the cane.
I'll keep only one point of contact with the floor at a time.

questions.explanation: The cane is held on the stronger, unaffected side — here, the right hand, since the injury is on the left. Two points of support should stay on the floor at all times.

questions.prompt: A nurse assesses a client using a Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. The client takes 15 seconds to complete the test. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Identify the client as being at increased risk for falls
Document the finding as a normal result
Discontinue further mobility assessment
Encourage the client to ambulate independently without supervision

questions.explanation: A TUG time greater than 12 seconds in an older adult indicates an increased fall risk, prompting the nurse to implement fall precautions.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who was just diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Position the client in high-Fowler's
Position the client supine and flat
Encourage the client to ambulate in the hallway
Apply a heating pad to the chest

questions.explanation: High-Fowler's positioning is prioritized for a client with a PE to promote optimal lung expansion and gas exchange while awaiting further treatment.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about positions that help prevent complications of immobility. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lying prone helps prevent contractures in the hips and knees.
options.rationale: Prone positioning fully extends the hips and knees, which helps prevent contractures.

options.text: The Trendelenburg position helps drain the lower lobes of your lungs.
options.rationale: With the foot of the bed raised, gravity helps drain the lower lung lobes.

options.text: Lying flat on your back is best for preventing pressure injuries.
options.rationale: Lying flat keeps pressure on the sacrum and heels; regular repositioning prevents pressure injury.

options.text: Side-lying with your hips and knees fully extended keeps your spine aligned.
options.rationale: In side-lying, the hips and knees are flexed with a pillow between the legs for alignment.

options.text: Fowler's position helps your lungs expand more fully.
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed lets the diaphragm move down so the lungs expand.

questions.explanation: Prone prevents hip and knee contractures, Trendelenburg drains the lower lung lobes, and Fowler's promotes lung expansion. Side-lying keeps the hips and knees flexed with a pillow between the legs, and lying flat does not by itself prevent pressure injury; repositioning does.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing range-of-motion exercises with an assistive personnel (AP). Which statement by the AP indicates an understanding of passive ROM?

options.text: I move the client's joints through their range of motion for them.
I encourage the client to move their own joints without my help.
Passive ROM will build the client's muscle strength the same as active ROM.
I only perform ROM exercises if the client requests them.

questions.explanation: Passive ROM is performed by the caregiver for the client, who does not participate; active ROM is performed by the client independently. Passive ROM helps maintain joint mobility but does not build muscle strength or prevent bone loss the way active, participatory movement does.

questions.prompt: A nurse applies an ice pack to a client's swollen ankle. Fifteen minutes later, the client reports numbness and the skin appears mottled. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Remove the ice pack immediately
Reapply the ice pack for another 15 minutes
Document the finding and check again in 1 hour
Apply a warm compress on top of the ice pack

questions.explanation: Numbness and mottling are signs of tissue damage from cold therapy — the application should be discontinued immediately.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about the use of sequential compression devices (SCDs). Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: The device will keep the blood pumping through your legs to help prevent clots.
The device will prevent pressure injuries on your skin.
The device will keep your leg muscles from becoming weak.
The device will keep your joints flexible.

questions.explanation: SCDs promote venous return and help prevent clot formation by mimicking the muscle-pump action that moves blood back to the heart.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client's synovial joints as part of a musculoskeletal exam. Which finding should the nurse identify as expected?

options.text: Smooth, pain-free movement of the joint through its range
Grinding sensation with movement
Joint swelling and warmth
Inability to bear weight

questions.explanation: Synovial joints normally allow smooth, flexible movement. Grinding, swelling/warmth, or inability to bear weight are abnormal findings requiring further assessment.

questions.prompt: A charge nurse is teaching a nursing student about how nerve cells contribute to movement. Which statement should the charge nurse include?

options.text: Nerve cells in the spinal cord signal muscles to contract, which pulls on the bones to create movement.
Nerve cells store calcium that strengthens bones.
Nerve cells produce the collagen found in tendons.
Nerve cells generate the heat muscles produce.

questions.explanation: Nerve cells in the spinal cord fire signals that cause muscles to contract; as muscles shorten, they pull against the bones they're attached to, generating movement.

questions.prompt: A nursing student is describing the role of cartilage. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: Cartilage lets the ends of my bones glide over each other without grinding.
Cartilage connects my muscles directly to my bones.
Cartilage produces red blood cells.
Cartilage sends nerve signals to my muscles.

questions.explanation: Cartilage reduces friction between bones, allowing them to glide smoothly and absorb shock.

questions.prompt: A nurse observes a colleague lifting a heavy box by bending at the waist with straight knees. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Remind the colleague to bend the knees and use the leg muscles
Allow the colleague to continue since the box is already lifted
Wait until after the task to mention proper technique
Report the colleague to the manager immediately

questions.explanation: Correcting unsafe body mechanics in the moment helps prevent an acute back injury; the nurse should intervene promptly rather than waiting or escalating unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching new staff about ergonomic risk factors in the workplace. Which examples should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Side-opening linen bins
options.rationale: Side-opening bins reduce bending and reaching, so they lower ergonomic risk.

options.text: A height-adjustable bed
options.rationale: A height-adjustable bed lets staff work at a safe height, which reduces strain.

options.text: Repetitive lifting without breaks
options.rationale: Repeated lifting without rest fatigues muscles and raises the risk of injury.

options.text: A wide, stable base when standing
options.rationale: A wide base of support improves balance and is good body mechanics.

options.text: Whole-body vibration from equipment
options.rationale: Whole-body vibration places stress on the spine and is an ergonomic risk factor.

questions.explanation: Repetitive lifting without breaks and whole-body vibration are ergonomic risk factors. Height-adjustable beds, side-opening linen bins, and a wide stable base are examples of good ergonomic practice.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client's family member about using a gait belt safely. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: I should be able to slip my fingers under the belt once it's fastened.
I should fasten the belt as tightly as possible with no space underneath.
The belt should be placed over bare skin only.
The belt is only used for clients who can walk independently.

questions.explanation: A gait belt should be snug but allow the caregiver to slip fingers underneath for safety and adjustment; it should not be applied so tight that there's no space.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client on bed rest who has not had a bowel movement in 4 days and reports abdominal discomfort. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Auscultate bowel sounds and palpate the abdomen
Administer a laxative without further assessment
Encourage the client to increase activity immediately
Document the finding and reassess in 24 hours

questions.explanation: The nurse should assess bowel sounds and the abdomen for distention or discomfort before intervening, to help determine whether this is simple constipation or a more serious complication like impaction.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about why bed rest increases the risk of pneumonia. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: Shallow breathing and thickened secretions make it harder to clear your lungs.
Bed rest increases the depth of your breaths.
Lying flat improves the effectiveness of your cough.
Bed rest has no effect on your risk for lung infections.

questions.explanation: Supine positioning decreases breathing depth and coughing effectiveness, and dehydration thickens secretions — together these raise the risk of pneumonia.

questions.prompt: A client asks the nurse why they need to reposition every 2 hours. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: Changing position keeps the pressure off any one area of my skin for too long.
Repositioning helps me digest my food faster.
Repositioning prevents my blood pressure from dropping when I stand.
Changing position helps my bones absorb more calcium.

questions.explanation: Frequent repositioning relieves prolonged pressure on bony prominences, reducing the risk of pressure injury.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client on bed rest for 1 week. Which findings should the nurse identify as expected complications of immobility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reports of new leg weakness
Increased appetite
Reddened area over the sacrum
Reports of feeling short of breath with minimal exertion
Improved bowel regularity

questions.explanation: Muscle weakness, skin breakdown over bony prominences, and decreased activity tolerance/dyspnea are all expected complications of immobility. Increased appetite and improved bowel regularity are not — immobility typically decreases appetite and causes constipation.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client who can sit on the edge of the bed with feet on the floor and extend one leg but cannot maintain a standing position. According to the BMAT, which level should the nurse assign?

options.text: Level 2, moderate assist
Level 1, maximum assist
Level 3, minimal assist
Level 4, no assist

questions.explanation: A client who can perform the Level 2 tasks (sitting with feet on floor, extending the leg) but cannot progress to standing independently is assigned Level 2, moderate assist.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who is starting a cardiac rehabilitation program how to use the Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: I will use this scale to rate how hard you appear to be working based on your breathing and color.
You will use this scale to rate how hard the activity feels to you, from very light to maximal effort.
This scale uses your heart rate and blood pressure to calculate your exercise intensity.
This scale measures how far you can walk before needing to rest.

questions.explanation: The Borg RPE scale is a subjective tool the client uses to rate how hard an activity feels to them, from very light to maximal effort, rather than a measurement based on the nurse's observation, vital signs, or distance walked.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client how to safely use axillary crutches. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll support my weight through my hands on the grips, not under my arms.
I'll rest my body weight on the crutch pads under my arms.
I'll keep my elbows locked straight when using the grips.
I'll place the crutches directly under my arms for the most support.

questions.explanation: Weight should be supported at the hand grips, never in the axilla — bearing weight on the crutch pads can cause nerve damage (crutch palsy).

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client with a stage 2 pressure injury on the sacrum. Which position should the nurse avoid for extended periods?

options.text: Supine with prolonged pressure on the sacrum
Left lateral with a pillow between the knees
Prone with pillows supporting the hips
Right lateral with heels elevated off the bed

questions.explanation: Prolonged supine positioning places direct, sustained pressure on the sacrum, worsening an existing pressure injury there; lateral or prone positioning off-loads that area.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching an assistive personnel about the purpose of a slide board for client transfers. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: A slide board creates a bridge so the client can slide sideways between two level surfaces without being lifted.
A slide board is used to help the client come to a full standing position before pivoting.
A slide board replaces the need for a gait belt when transferring a client.
A slide board is used to reposition a client up in bed when they have slid toward the foot of the bed.

questions.explanation: A slide board bridges two level surfaces (such as a bed and stretcher) so an immobile client can be slid across laterally without staff lifting their full weight. It is not used for standing pivot transfers, as a gait belt replacement, or for repositioning a client up in bed.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client the purpose of the Trendelenburg position. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: Having the foot of my bed higher than my head helps blood return to my heart.
This position helps my lungs expand more fully.
This position takes pressure off my hips and sacrum.
This position helps prevent contractures in my knees.

questions.explanation: The Trendelenburg position (foot of bed higher than head) promotes venous return and drainage of the lower lung lobes.

questions.prompt: A nurse is selecting a position for a client recovering from abdominal surgery who reports difficulty taking deep breaths. Which position characteristics should the nurse prioritize? Select all that apply.

options.text: Head of bed elevated 45 degrees
options.rationale: Fowler's position at 45 degrees lowers the abdominal organs off the diaphragm so the lungs can expand.

options.text: Foot of bed elevated above the head
options.rationale: Trendelenburg pushes the abdominal organs toward the diaphragm, making deep breaths harder.

options.text: Lying flat with head turned to one side
options.rationale: Lying flat does not help lung expansion for a client who is struggling to breathe deeply.

options.text: Semi-seated positioning
options.rationale: A semi-seated position promotes lung expansion and easier deep breathing.

options.text: Full extension of the hips and knees
options.rationale: Full hip and knee extension prevents contractures but does not improve breathing and may strain an abdominal incision.

questions.explanation: Fowler's-type positioning (head of bed elevated, semi-seated) promotes lung expansion, which helps a client having difficulty breathing deeply. Trendelenburg, lying flat, and full hip and knee extension do not address this need.

questions.prompt: A nurse is applying a warm compress to a client's abdomen who has a heating pad prescription. The nurse notes the client has an implanted pacemaker. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Avoid placing the heat application directly over the device
Apply the heat application as prescribed without changes
Increase the temperature of the heat application
Apply the heat application for a longer duration than prescribed

questions.explanation: Heat should not be applied directly over metal medical devices such as pacemakers or prosthetic joints, as this can cause deep tissue burns.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about ankle pump exercises. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: Point your toes toward your head, then away from your head, to help pump blood back to your heart.
These exercises are meant to strengthen your grip.
Perform these exercises only once a day.
These exercises replace the need for compression stockings.

questions.explanation: Ankle pumps (pointing toes toward and away from the head) contract the calf muscles, which helps promote venous return — they're recommended hourly while awake, not just once daily, and don't replace prescribed compression devices.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who had a suspected DVT identified in one leg. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: I should avoid massaging or rubbing the affected area.
I should massage the area to help break up the clot.
I should keep the leg lower than my heart.
I should apply firm pressure to the area throughout the day.

questions.explanation: Massaging or applying pressure to a suspected clot can dislodge it, risking a pulmonary embolism; the leg should instead be elevated and the provider notified.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who is on prolonged bed rest. Which interventions help prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT)? Move the correct interventions to the answer box.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices (SCDs)
options.rationale: SCDs squeeze the legs to push blood back toward the heart.

options.text: Teach ankle flexing and foot circles
options.rationale: Lower-leg exercises work the calf muscles and reduce venous stasis.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids
options.rationale: Fluids keep the blood from getting thick.

options.text: Apply antiembolism stockings as prescribed
options.rationale: Antiembolism stockings promote venous return.

options.text: Massage the client's calves
options.rationale: Massaging the calves could dislodge a clot.

options.text: Encourage use of an incentive spirometer
options.rationale: The incentive spirometer prevents atelectasis, not DVT.

options.text: Increase fiber in the diet
options.rationale: Fiber prevents constipation, not DVT.

questions.summary: Keep blood moving out of the legs: stockings, SCDs, leg exercises, fluids, ambulation, and anticoagulants as prescribed.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reinforcing teaching with a client who has a new standard walker and a weak left leg. Which instructions should the nurse include? Move the correct instructions to the answer box.

options.text: Move the walker first, then step with the left leg
options.rationale: Move the walker, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg.

options.text: The top of the walker should line up with your wrist
options.rationale: The top of the walker sits at the wrist.

options.text: Your elbows should bend about 15 degrees when you hold the grips
options.rationale: A walker uses about 15° of elbow bend.

options.text: Wear nonskid footwear
options.rationale: Nonskid footwear is part of safe ambulation.

options.text: Step with the right leg first after moving the walker
options.rationale: The weaker (left) leg moves first after the walker, not the stronger one.

options.text: Use the walker to go up and down stairs
options.rationale: Walkers are never used on stairs or escalators.

options.text: Your elbows should bend 20 to 30 degrees when you hold the grips
options.rationale: 20–30° is for canes and crutches. The walker is 15°.

questions.summary: Walker, weak leg, strong leg. Top at the wrist, elbows at 15°, never on stairs.

questions.prompt: A nurse enters a client's room to start an IV catheter. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply alcohol-based hand sanitizer
Wash hands with soap and water for 5 seconds
Put on gloves without performing hand hygiene
Ask the client to leave the room

questions.explanation: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer should be used just before touching a client or performing a sterile technique like IV insertion, unless hands are visibly soiled.

questions.prompt: A charge nurse is teaching a nursing student about the layers of the skin. Which statement by the student requires further teaching?

options.text: The epidermis has its own blood supply.
The dermis contains nerves that sense pressure.
The hypodermis stores fat that insulates the body.
The epidermis is the outermost layer.

questions.explanation: The epidermis is avascular (has no blood vessels) and receives nutrition from the dermis below it — this statement is incorrect and indicates a need for further teaching.

questions.prompt: A nursing student is explaining Langerhans cells to a classmate. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: They travel through the body and help activate the immune response to pathogens on the skin.
They produce collagen in the dermis.
They form the hard enamel coating on teeth.
They store fat in the hypodermis.

questions.explanation: Langerhans cells are found in the skin and participate in the early immune response by detecting invaders.

questions.prompt: A nurse removes gloves after providing wound care. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Perform hand hygiene
Document the wound care
Move directly to the next client's room
Reapply a new pair of gloves

questions.explanation: Hand hygiene should be performed immediately after glove removal, before any other task, to prevent pathogen transmission.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about HAIs (health care–associated infections). Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: An HAI is an infection that develops after you're admitted to the hospital and wasn't present when you arrived.
An HAI is any infection you have before being admitted.
HAIs only occur in the intensive care unit.
HAIs cannot be prevented through hand hygiene.

questions.explanation: HAIs develop during a client's stay in a health care facility and were not present on admission; hand hygiene is a key prevention strategy.

questions.prompt: A charge nurse asks a nursing student why mucous membranes are important. Which statement by the student shows understanding?

options.text: They line passages like the respiratory and digestive tract and trap pathogens with mucus.
They only protect the skin from sunburn.
They produce the hard enamel on teeth.
They store calcium for the bones.

questions.explanation: Mucous membranes line body passages open to the outside environment and secrete mucus that traps pathogens and particles.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to bathe a client who cannot ambulate to the bathroom. Which type of bath should the nurse anticipate providing?

options.text: Complete bed bath
Therapeutic bath
Partial bath only
No bath is needed

questions.explanation: A complete bed bath is given to clients unable to ambulate to the bathroom and bathe themselves.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a new assistive personnel about bathing a client at risk for DVT. Which statement requires further teaching?

options.text: I'll use firm, deep strokes over the lower extremities.
I'll wash the arms distal to proximal.
I'll use light strokes over the lower extremities.
I'll change the water if it becomes cool or soapy.

questions.explanation: Firm, deep strokes should be avoided over the lower extremities of a client with a history of DVT; light strokes are used instead to avoid dislodging a clot.

questions.prompt: A nurse educator is teaching about CHG bathing. Which statement by a new nurse indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll massage the CHG cloths over all of the client's skin except the face.
I'll apply CHG cloths only to the client's face.
CHG bathing replaces the need for hand hygiene.
CHG bathing is only used for ambulatory clients.

questions.explanation: CHG (chlorhexidine gluconate) bathing involves massaging premoistened cloths over all skin except the face, and is commonly used to reduce infection risk in high-risk units like the ICU.

questions.prompt: A nurse is washing a client's arm during a bed bath. Which technique should the nurse use?

options.text: Wash from the hand toward the shoulder
Wash from the shoulder toward the hand
Wash in random, circular motions
Wash only the palm of the hand

questions.explanation: Washing distal to proximal (hand toward shoulder) facilitates venous blood return.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has deep skin folds related to a higher body weight. Which nursing actions should the nurse plan to include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash the skin folds with a pH-balanced liquid soap
options.rationale: Washing removes trapped sweat, and pH-balanced soap is gentle on the skin.

options.text: Leave the skin folds moist to prevent irritation
options.rationale: Moisture trapped in skin folds causes rashes and infection.

options.text: Lightly dab the skin dry after washing
options.rationale: Dabbing dries the folds without causing friction damage.

options.text: Rub the skin folds briskly with a towel to dry them
options.rationale: Brisk rubbing causes friction that can damage fragile skin; dab dry instead.

options.text: Avoid washing between skin folds
options.rationale: Skin folds trap sweat and need regular washing to prevent rash and infection.

questions.explanation: Skin folds should be washed with pH-balanced liquid soap and gently dabbed dry. Leaving them moist, skipping washing, or rubbing them briskly increases the risk of rash, breakdown, and infection.

questions.prompt: A charge nurse is teaching a nursing student about the risk of using a bath basin during hospitalization. Which statement should the charge nurse include?

options.text: Bath basins have been shown to harbor pathogens that can spread between clients.
Bath basins eliminate the risk of skin breakdown.
Bath basins are always safer than no-rinse cleansing products.
Bath basins prevent the need for hand hygiene during bathing.

questions.explanation: Bath basins have been shown to be contaminated with pathogens and can aid in transferring them within a health care setting.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching about the order of a complete bed bath. Which statement by the student indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll wash the face first, then work from the trunk down to the lower extremities.
I'll wash the perineal area first to save time.
I'll wash the feet first, then work upward.
The order doesn't matter as long as everything gets washed.

questions.explanation: A bed bath follows a clean-to-dirty, head-to-toe order: face first, then trunk/upper extremities, then lower extremities, with perineal care typically performed last.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for an unconscious client who requires oral hygiene. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Position the client on their side with the head turned toward the mattress
Place two fingers in the client's mouth to hold it open
Provide oral care with the client positioned flat on their back
Skip oral care since the client is unconscious

questions.explanation: Positioning an unconscious client on their side with the head turned toward the mattress allows secretions to drain out and reduces aspiration risk before beginning oral care.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about denture care. Which statement by the client requires further teaching?

options.text: I'll brush my dentures with my regular toothpaste.
I'll store my dentures in a labeled cup with water.
I'll handle my dentures carefully since they can break.
I'll rinse my dentures with cool water after brushing.

questions.explanation: Regular toothpaste is abrasive and can damage denture surfaces; denture-specific toothpaste should be used instead.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a nursing student how to remove a client's upper denture. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll pull the upper denture down and out at the front to break the seal.
I'll push the upper denture up and out at the front.
I'll pull the upper denture straight back toward the throat.
I'll twist the upper denture side to side.

questions.explanation: The upper denture is removed by pulling down and out at the front, which breaks the seal between the denture and the roof of the mouth.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client on a ventilator. Which actions should the nurse take to help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform regular oral hygiene, including brushing the teeth
options.rationale: Brushing removes plaque and bacteria that can be carried into the lungs and cause VAP.

options.text: Withhold mouth care while the client is intubated to avoid moving the tube
options.rationale: Intubated clients need regular nurse-provided mouth care; skipping it lets bacteria build up.

options.text: Use lemon-glycerin swabs as the main method of mouth care
options.rationale: Lemon-glycerin swabs dry the mouth and do not remove plaque the way brushing does.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 10 degrees or lower
options.rationale: A nearly flat position raises aspiration risk; the head of the bed is usually kept at 30 to 45 degrees.

options.text: Apply lip moisturizer in place of brushing the teeth
options.rationale: Lip moisturizer protects the lips but does nothing to remove bacteria from the teeth and mouth.

questions.explanation: Regular nurse-provided oral hygiene, including brushing, lowers the mouth bacteria that can travel into the lungs along the artificial airway. Mouth care must not be skipped or replaced with lip products, lemon-glycerin swabs dry the mouth, and the head of the bed should be raised, not kept flat.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assisting a client with fragile oral mucosa to brush their teeth. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Use gentle brushing and flossing technique
Use a firm-bristle toothbrush for a more thorough clean
Brush vigorously to remove all plaque quickly
Avoid oral care altogether to prevent bleeding

questions.explanation: Clients with fragile oral mucosa require gentle brushing and flossing to clean effectively without causing trauma or bleeding.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about gingivitis. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: It's inflammation of the gums caused by plaque buildup, and it can progress to a more serious infection if untreated.
It's a hardening of the tooth enamel.
It only affects clients who wear dentures.
It's unrelated to oral hygiene habits.

questions.explanation: Gingivitis is gum inflammation from plaque caused by poor oral hygiene, and can progress to periodontitis if not addressed.

questions.prompt: A nurse is providing oral care for a client who can participate independently. Which actions should the nurse encourage the client to perform? Select all that apply.

options.text: Brush all surfaces of the teeth, front and back
Brush the surface of the tongue
Skip flossing since brushing is sufficient
Rinse with mouthwash after brushing and flossing
Avoid rinsing with water after brushing

questions.explanation: Brushing all tooth surfaces and the tongue, followed by flossing and a mouthwash rinse, are all recommended oral hygiene steps for an independent client.

questions.prompt: A nurse is providing foot care for a client who has diabetes mellitus and a history of peripheral neuropathy. Which action should the nurse avoid?

options.text: Soaking the client's feet in a basin of water
Washing the feet with warm water and mild soap
Drying thoroughly between the toes
Inspecting the feet for redness or cuts

questions.explanation: Soaking the feet of a client with neuropathy or diabetes should be avoided — it can cause maceration and softening of the skin, increasing infection risk.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client with diabetes about foot care. Which statement by the client requires further teaching?

options.text: I'll apply lotion between my toes to keep the skin soft.
I'll wear clean cotton socks every day.
I'll check my shoes for objects or rough seams before putting them on.
I'll cut my toenails straight across.

questions.explanation: Lotion should never be applied between the toes — the added moisture increases the risk of fungal infection.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about nail hygiene. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: Keeping my nails trimmed short helps reduce the germs that build up underneath them.
Longer nails are cleaner because there's more surface to wash.
Nail length doesn't affect how many germs are on my hands.
I should round the edges of my nails as much as possible when trimming.

questions.explanation: Longer nails have been shown to harbor more germs than shorter nails; trimming nails short and cleaning underneath is recommended.

questions.prompt: A nurse is inspecting a client's feet during a routine assessment. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: A small cut between the toes
Even coloring on both feet
A blister on the heel
Cracked, dry skin on both heels
Warm, dry skin with no lesions

questions.explanation: Cuts, blisters, and cracked skin are abnormal findings that increase infection risk and should be reported. Even coloring and warm, intact, dry skin are normal findings.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to trim a client's toenails. Facility policy requires a podiatrist to trim nails for clients with diabetes. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Refer the client to a podiatrist for nail trimming
Trim the nails as requested by the client
Soak the feet and trim the nails regardless of policy
Delegate the task to unlicensed assistive personnel

questions.explanation: When facility policy restricts nail trimming for at-risk clients, such as those with diabetes, to a qualified professional, the nurse should follow that policy and refer accordingly.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about proper toenail trimming technique. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll cut my toenails straight across and file any sharp edges.
I'll round the corners of my toenails when trimming.
I'll cut my toenails as short as possible, close to the skin.
I'll avoid filing any rough edges after trimming.

questions.explanation: Cutting toenails straight across and filing sharp edges reduces the risk of ingrown toenails.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has a known open wound on the foot and a prescription for foot care. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Consult with the health care team before immersing the foot in a water basin
Immerse the foot in warm water as routinely done
Apply lotion directly into the open wound
Skip the consultation and proceed with standard foot care

questions.explanation: For a client with a known wound, the nurse should confirm orders for wound care with the health care team before immersing the foot in water, since soaking may not be advisable.

questions.prompt: A nurse is performing perineal care for a female client. Which technique should the nurse use?

options.text: Clean from front to back
Clean from back to front
Clean in a random pattern
Clean using the same area of the washcloth for the entire procedure

questions.explanation: Perineal care for a female client should move front to back (anterior to posterior) to avoid moving bacteria from the rectal area toward the urethra.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a new nurse about perineal care for an uncircumcised male client. Which statement requires further teaching?

options.text: I'll leave the foreskin retracted after cleaning to allow it to air dry.
I'll retract the foreskin before cleaning underneath it.
I'll return the foreskin to its natural position after cleaning.
I'll clean the tip of the penis in a circular motion, working outward.

questions.explanation: The foreskin should always be returned to its natural position after cleaning — leaving it retracted can cause constriction, swelling, and pain.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about indwelling catheter care. Which statement indicates understanding of the correct order?

options.text: I'll clean the genital area first, then the meatus, then the catheter moving away from the body.
I'll clean the catheter first, then the meatus, then the genital area.
I'll clean all areas simultaneously with one pass of the washcloth.
I'll clean the catheter moving toward the body.

questions.explanation: Catheter care proceeds clean to dirty: genital area first, then the meatus where the catheter enters, then the catheter itself, cleaning away from the client's body.

questions.prompt: A nurse is gathering supplies to perform perineal care. Which items should the nurse obtain? Select all that apply.

options.text: Waterproof pad
Facility-approved perineal wipes or cleanser
Sterile gloves
Washcloths and towels
Cotton swabs

questions.explanation: A waterproof pad, cleanser/wipes, and washcloths/towels are standard perineal care supplies. Sterile gloves and cotton swabs are not required for routine perineal care.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to perform perineal care for a client and needs to determine positioning. Which position is ideal for a female client who is able to tolerate it?

options.text: Dorsal recumbent
Prone
High-Fowler's with legs extended straight
Left lateral only

questions.explanation: The dorsal recumbent position (lying on the back with knees bent) provides ideal access to the perineum for care, if the client is able to tolerate it.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a new nurse about perineal care technique for a female client. Which statement requires further teaching?

options.text: I'll use the same section of the washcloth for each downward pass over the labia.
I'll separate the labia with my nondominant hand to clean the labia minora.
I'll rinse the perineum and gently pat it dry when finished.
I'll wash the labia majora from front to back first.

questions.explanation: A new, unused section of the washcloth should be used for each downward pass to prevent spreading microorganisms — reusing the same section requires further teaching.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assisting a client who has left-sided weakness with changing into a hospital gown. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Remove the gown from the unaffected (right) side first
Remove the gown from the affected (left) side first
Place the clean gown on the unaffected (right) side first
Ask a family member to remove the gown instead

questions.explanation: When undressing, remove clothing from the unaffected (strong) side first; when dressing, dress the affected (weak) side first.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client with a spinal cord injury about safe bathing. Which statement should the nurse include?

options.text: Always check the water temperature carefully since you may have reduced ability to sense heat.
Water temperature doesn't need special attention.
You should bathe in water as hot as you can tolerate.
Reduced sensation only affects your ability to feel cold water.

questions.explanation: Spinal cord injuries can impair the ability to sense temperature, increasing the risk of burns — water temperature should always be checked carefully before bathing.

questions.prompt: A nurse reviews a client's notes. 0700: Client has dementia, refuses morning shower, becomes agitated when approached about bathing. 0730: Client is calm and cooperative after breakfast. Based on this information, which approach should the nurse try next?

options.text: Offer to bathe the client on the commode after their next bowel movement, when calmer
Insist the client shower immediately at 0700 as originally scheduled
Document the refusal and skip bathing for the entire week
Physically guide the client to the shower against their wishes

questions.explanation: For clients with dementia, adapting the timing and method of bathing — such as bathing on the commode after a bowel movement, when the client is calmer — supports dignity and cooperation rather than forcing care during agitation.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has a visual impairment how to shave safely. Which instruction should the nurse include first?

options.text: Explore the facial contours with the fingers before beginning
Begin shaving immediately using long strokes
Use a razor with the blade exposed while practicing
Ask a family member to perform the shaving instead

questions.explanation: The client should first explore their facial contours to identify areas needing shaving, then practice with the razor turned off before shaving, to build safety and confidence.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a caregiver about hygiene care for a client who has had an arm amputation. Which statement by the caregiver indicates understanding?

options.text: I'll place a bath seat in the shower and add a grab bar for support.
I'll avoid using any adaptive devices to encourage full independence right away.
I'll discourage the use of a battery-powered toothbrush.
I'll remove all anti-slip mats from the bathroom floor.

questions.explanation: A bath seat and grab bars support safe transfers and bathing for a client adjusting to limb loss; adaptive devices like battery-powered toothbrushes and anti-slip mats also help maintain safety and independence.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to provide daily care for a client who has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which supplies should the nurse gather? Move the correct supplies to the answer box.

options.text: Washcloths
options.rationale: Washcloths are used to clean the genitals, meatus, and catheter.

options.text: Skin cleanser
options.rationale: Skin cleanser is used for daily catheter care.

options.text: Skin protectant cream
options.rationale: Skin protectant cream protects the perineal skin.

options.text: Waterproof pad
options.rationale: A waterproof pad keeps the bed dry during care.

options.text: Cotton swabs
options.rationale: Cotton swabs aren't used for catheter care.

options.text: Hydrogen peroxide
options.rationale: Peroxide isn't used for catheter care.

options.text: Povidone-iodine
options.rationale: Povidone-iodine isn't used for routine catheter care.

options.text: Sterile gloves
options.rationale: Daily catheter care uses clean gloves, not sterile ones.

questions.summary: Clean genitals → meatus → catheter, moving away from the body, with clean gloves.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing hand hygiene. In which situations should the nurse use soap and water instead of alcohol-based hand sanitizer? Move the correct situations to the answer box.

options.text: The nurse's hands are visibly soiled
options.rationale: Soiled: sanitizer can't remove visible dirt.

options.text: After caring for a client who has C. difficile
options.rationale: Spores: sanitizer doesn't kill C. difficile spores, so wash with soap and water.

options.text: After caring for a client who has infectious diarrhea
options.rationale: Stool: infectious diarrhea calls for soap and water.

options.text: Before touching a client
options.rationale: Sanitizer is the default before touching a client.

options.text: Right after removing clean gloves
options.rationale: Sanitizer is used right after removing gloves unless hands are soiled.

options.text: Before performing sterile technique
options.rationale: Sanitizer is used before sterile technique.

questions.summary: Soap for the 3 S's: soiled, stool, spores.

questions.prompt: A nurse is educating a client with a new stoma. The client watches the nurse change the pouch for the first time. Which stage of the psychomotor domain is the client demonstrating?

options.text: Perception
Mechanism
Adaptation
Origination

questions.explanation: Perception is the first psychomotor stage — the client observes the nurse performing the skill before attempting it themselves.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about their new diagnosis. The client says, 'I understand I have diabetes, but I'm still upset about needing daily injections.' Which domain of learning is this statement primarily reflecting?

options.text: Affective
Cognitive
Psychomotor
Sensory

questions.explanation: The affective domain involves feelings, values, and beliefs — the client's emotional reaction to the diagnosis reflects this domain, separate from factual knowledge (cognitive) or hands-on skill (psychomotor).

questions.prompt: A nurse is planning teaching strategies based on the psychomotor domain. Which strategies should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Demonstration
Lecture
Return demonstration
Question-and-answer
Games

questions.explanation: Demonstration, return demonstration, and games are psychomotor domain strategies. Lecture and question-and-answer belong to the cognitive domain.

questions.prompt: A nurse is evaluating whether a client has achieved cognitive learning about hypoglycemia. Which finding best demonstrates this?

options.text: The client verbalizes the signs of hypoglycemia and when to call the provider
The client demonstrates checking their own blood sugar
The client expresses feelings about their diagnosis
The client asks no questions during teaching

questions.explanation: Verbalizing knowledge (recall and comprehension) demonstrates cognitive learning; performing a skill demonstrates psychomotor learning, and expressing feelings demonstrates affective learning.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client with a new colostomy and wants to address the affective domain. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Encourage the client to discuss their feelings about the change in body image
Have the client recite the steps to change the pouch
Ask the client to demonstrate emptying the pouch
Provide a written pamphlet on colostomy care

questions.explanation: Addressing feelings, values, and beliefs — such as body image concerns — engages the affective domain of learning.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about the cognitive domain. Which statement by the student indicates understanding?

options.text: The cognitive domain includes stages like knowledge, comprehension, and application.
The cognitive domain is only about physical skills.
The cognitive domain focuses on a client's emotions.
The cognitive domain has no measurable stages.

questions.explanation: The cognitive domain (the 'thinking domain') has 6 stages: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation.

questions.prompt: A client who has a new ostomy now changes the pouch consistently without error, and it has become part of their daily routine. Which psychomotor stage does this represent?

options.text: Origination
Perception
Guided response
Set

questions.explanation: Origination (naturalization) is the final psychomotor stage, where the skill becomes part of the client's normal routine.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who states, 'I don't see why I need to learn this.' Which Knowles principle should the nurse address first?

options.text: Relevance/need to know
Self-directed
Life experience
Task-centered

questions.explanation: The client's statement reflects a lack of understanding of why the information matters to them — the nurse should first address the relevance/need-to-know principle before proceeding with teaching.

questions.prompt: A nurse is applying Knowles's principle of readiness when planning teaching for a client. Which statement should guide the nurse's approach?

options.text: I should assess whether the client is willing and able to actively engage before teaching.
I should teach regardless of the client's current emotional state.
Readiness only applies to pediatric clients.
Readiness means the client has already mastered the material.

questions.explanation: Readiness means the client is willing, able, and can actively engage in learning — the nurse should assess this before beginning teaching.

questions.prompt: A client says, 'I've managed my father's diabetes for years, so I think I can handle learning to manage my own.' Which Knowles principle does this statement reflect?

options.text: Life experience
Readiness
Relevance
Motivation

questions.explanation: The client is using past personal experience as a foundation for new learning, reflecting the life experience principle.

questions.prompt: A client with newly diagnosed hypertension states they understand the risks of not taking their medication but still refuses to commit to the regimen. Which Knowles principle is most clearly unmet?

options.text: Motivation
Life experience
Task-centered
Relevance

questions.explanation: The client has the knowledge (relevance is understood) but lacks internal motivation, which must be present for real behavior change and learning to take place.

questions.prompt: A nurse is applying Knowles's adult learning principles when developing a teaching plan. Which actions reflect these principles? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explaining why the information is relevant to the client's specific situation
options.rationale: Adults learn best when they know why the information applies to them.

options.text: Ignoring the client's past experiences with similar health conditions
options.rationale: Adult learning builds on what the client already knows.

options.text: Having the nurse decide when and how the client will practice new skills
options.rationale: Adults are self-directed and should control choices about their own learning.

options.text: Presenting information only as material to memorize
options.rationale: Adult learning is task-centered and tied to real problems, not memorization.

options.text: Linking teaching to the client's real-life tasks and problems
options.rationale: Task-centered teaching connects learning to the client's real problems.

questions.explanation: Explaining relevance and using task-centered teaching reflect Knowles's principles. Adults are self-directed and should make their own choices, and teaching should build on past experience rather than ignore it or rely on rote memorization.

questions.prompt: A nursing student explains self-directed learning to a classmate. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: Self-directed clients take responsibility for their choices and have control over their learning.
Self-directed learning means the nurse makes all the decisions.
Self-directed learning applies only to children.
Self-directed clients require no assessment before teaching.

questions.explanation: Self-directed clients participate in their own learning and accept responsibility for their choices and consequences.

questions.prompt: A nurse is beginning to develop a teaching plan for a client newly diagnosed with diabetes. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Assess the client's learning needs, readiness, and health literacy
Develop a written pamphlet on insulin administration
Ask the client to return-demonstrate a glucose check
Document that teaching was completed

questions.explanation: Assessment — gathering data on learning needs, readiness, and health literacy — is the first step of the teaching process before planning or implementing teaching.

questions.prompt: A nurse is writing a SMART outcome goal for a client learning to self-administer insulin. Which goal best meets SMART criteria?

options.text: Client will independently draw up and administer insulin correctly by the time of discharge.
Client will feel more comfortable with insulin.
Client will learn about insulin eventually.
Client will understand diabetes management.

questions.explanation: This goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and timed (by discharge), meeting all SMART criteria. The other options are vague and not measurable or time-bound.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a client to explain, in their own words, the signs of low blood sugar. Which element of the teaching process is the nurse performing?

options.text: Evaluation
Assessment
Planning
Implementation

questions.explanation: Asking the client to explain material in their own words (teach-back) is a method of evaluation, determining whether the learning goal was met.

questions.prompt: A client has not met the learning goal of independently checking their blood glucose after two teaching sessions. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Determine if the goal is realistic and consider new teaching strategies
Document that the client is noncompliant and stop teaching
Assume the client will never learn the skill
Repeat the exact same teaching method a third time without changes

questions.explanation: If a learning goal is unmet, the nurse should evaluate whether the goal is realistic and whether new teaching methods, based on the client's learning style, are needed.

questions.prompt: A nurse is implementing a teaching plan for a client learning to manage a new colostomy. Which strategies reflect a multimodal, multisensory approach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Providing verbal discussion of the steps
Using only one static approach for every client
Demonstrating the skill for the client
Giving the client printed materials to review
Offering a video resource

questions.explanation: A multimodal approach combines verbal discussion, demonstration, printed materials, and videos, reinforced with teach-back, not a single static method repeated for every client.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about the difference between the teaching process and the nursing process. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: The teaching process focuses on the client's learning needs, while the nursing process focuses on overall health care needs.
The teaching process and nursing process are identical in focus.
The nursing process only applies to physical care, never education.
The teaching process has no relationship to the nursing process.

questions.explanation: Both processes share similar steps (assessment, planning, implementation, evaluation), but the teaching process specifically targets the client's learning needs, motivation, and ability to learn.

questions.prompt: A nurse is planning diabetes education for six newly diagnosed clients on the unit. Which teaching strategy is most appropriate for this group size?

options.text: Group instruction, since six or fewer people is considered ideal for group teaching
Individual instruction only, since groups are never appropriate
Role play only
Digital technology only, with no other methods

questions.explanation: Group instruction is often most effective with six people or fewer, which fits this group size for shared teaching such as a diabetes education session.

questions.prompt: A nurse is using teach-back with a client after providing wound care instructions. Which statement should the nurse use?

options.text: Can you tell me, in your own words, how you'll care for this wound at home?
Do you understand everything I just said?
I'll just repeat the instructions one more time.
You don't need to explain it back to me.

questions.explanation: Teach-back involves asking the client to explain the information in their own words, which allows the nurse to evaluate true understanding rather than a simple yes/no response.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about the benefits of digital resources for learning about their new medication. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?

options.text: Using an app alongside your teaching can help reinforce what I've learned.
Digital tools should completely replace talking with my nurse.
Digital resources are never reliable for health information.
I don't need any other teaching method if I use an app.

questions.explanation: Digital technology is most effective when combined with traditional teaching strategies, not used as a complete replacement.

questions.prompt: A nurse is choosing a teaching strategy for a client who has significant social anxiety and is uncomfortable in groups. Which approach should the nurse prioritize?

options.text: Individual instruction
A large group class
A support group setting
A public health seminar

questions.explanation: Group settings do not work well for all clients, especially when emotional barriers like social anxiety are present; individual instruction is more appropriate here.

questions.prompt: A nurse is identifying examples of group instruction. Which examples should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: A childbirth education class
One-on-one teaching at the bedside
A diabetes education clinic with multiple attendees
A support group session
Education during an individual outpatient clinic visit

questions.explanation: Childbirth classes, diabetes education clinics, and support groups are all group instruction examples. Bedside and individual clinic visit teaching are individual instruction.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to teach a client and notices the client appears to be in pain. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Address the client's pain before beginning the teaching session
Proceed with teaching as scheduled regardless of pain
Postpone teaching indefinitely without further assessment
Ask a family member to receive the teaching instead

questions.explanation: Physical discomfort is a barrier to learning; addressing pain first helps create conditions where the client can actually engage with and retain the teaching.

questions.prompt: A nurse is applying the AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions when teaching all clients. Which approach should the nurse use?

options.text: Treat every client as if they may have difficulty understanding health information, using plain language
Assume only clients with a low education level need simplified language
Use medical terminology to ensure accuracy
Avoid checking for understanding unless the client asks questions

questions.explanation: The Universal Precautions approach means treating all clients as potentially having limited health literacy, using plain language and confirming understanding regardless of assumptions about education level.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about factors that support learning. Which statement by the client reflects understanding of a low-stimulus environment?

options.text: A quiet room with good lighting and a comfortable temperature will help me focus during teaching.
Learning works best with background noise and distractions.
The room temperature doesn't affect my ability to learn.
I learn better in a crowded, busy area.

questions.explanation: A low-stimulus environment — quiet, well-lit, comfortable temperature, minimal distractions — supports better learning outcomes.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client for barriers to learning before a teaching session. Which findings should the nurse identify as potential barriers? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client reports high anxiety about their diagnosis
The client has a strong support system
The client has a hearing impairment
The client reports significant pain
The client is fluent in the nurse's primary language

questions.explanation: Anxiety, hearing impairment, and pain are all recognized barriers to learning. A strong support system and shared language are facilitators, not barriers.

questions.prompt: A nurse is distinguishing fine motor skills from gross motor skills while planning teaching for a client with reduced hand dexterity. Which task would be most affected?

options.text: Buttoning a shirt
Walking across the room
Performing range-of-motion exercises
Self-propelling a wheelchair

questions.explanation: Buttoning a shirt is a fine motor skill requiring dexterity of small muscles, which would be most affected by reduced hand dexterity. The others are gross motor skills.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching about self-bias. Which statement by a new nurse indicates understanding?

options.text: I should reflect on my own thoughts and feelings before caring for clients from backgrounds different from mine.
Self-bias doesn't affect the quality of care I provide.
I don't need to consider my own perceptions when teaching clients.
Self-bias only applies to clients, not nurses.

questions.explanation: Reflecting on personal thoughts and feelings helps nurses identify and reduce self-bias before interacting with clients from diverse backgrounds.

questions.prompt: A nurse provides feedback to a client during a return demonstration of blood pressure self-monitoring. Which purpose does this feedback serve?

options.text: It helps the nurse evaluate the client's understanding and identify if more guidance is needed
It replaces the need for further teaching sessions
It is only useful after teaching is fully completed
It has no impact on the client's learning

questions.explanation: Feedback given during and after teaching helps the nurse assess the client's understanding and determine whether additional guidance is needed.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching an adolescent client about managing a new diagnosis. Which statement by the nurse reflects best practice for this age group?

options.text: Let's talk about how you can manage this — I'll answer any questions you have.
I'll only speak with your parents about your care.
I'll lecture you about all the things you're doing wrong.
Your privacy isn't a priority during this teaching.

questions.explanation: Teaching for adolescents should focus on the adolescent as the primary learner, use guidance rather than lecturing, and protect their modesty and privacy.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching an 80-year-old client with mild hearing and vision decline. Which approach should the nurse prioritize?

options.text: Reduce distractions, speak in a low tone, and present information in smaller segments
Speak quickly to cover all material in one session
Present all information at once in a single large block
Avoid repeating any information during teaching

questions.explanation: Older adults may process new information more slowly; reducing distractions, speaking clearly, allowing more time, and breaking information into smaller segments supports learning.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to teach a client whose primary language differs from the nurse's. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Arrange for a certified medical interpreter
Ask the client's adult child to interpret
Use only written English materials
Proceed with teaching in English without any interpretation

questions.explanation: A certified medical interpreter should always be used rather than a family member, to ensure accuracy and protect client confidentiality.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching about cultural considerations in client education. Which statement by a nursing student indicates understanding?

options.text: I should ask about the client's beliefs and preferences rather than assume based on their culture.
All clients from the same culture have identical health beliefs.
Cultural beliefs have no impact on how clients respond to teaching.
I should apply the same generalized approach to every client regardless of background.

questions.explanation: Nurses should assess each client's individual beliefs, customs, and values rather than generalizing based on culture, to avoid stereotyping and provide individualized, culturally sensitive education.

questions.prompt: A nurse is evaluating a client's readiness to learn about a new medication regimen. Which client statement indicates readiness to learn?

options.text: Can you show me how to take this new medication safely?
I really don't want to think about this right now.
I can't remember anything the doctor told me.
I'll worry about that after I feel better.

questions.explanation: A client actively requesting information and engaging with the material demonstrates readiness to learn, in contrast to statements reflecting avoidance or disengagement.

questions.prompt: A nurse is deciding between group and individual instruction for a client recovering from a highly stigmatized diagnosis who expresses discomfort discussing it in front of others. Which strategy should the nurse choose?

options.text: Individual instruction
A large support group
A public health class
A group session with unfamiliar peers

questions.explanation: When a client expresses discomfort or an emotional barrier to group settings, individual instruction is the more appropriate strategy.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching an older adult client who has mild cognitive decline about a new medication. Which approach should the nurse use?

options.text: Teach in short sessions and include a family member or caregiver
Cover all of the information in one long session so nothing is missed
Speak quickly in a higher-pitched voice to hold the client's attention
Give the client a written handout and let them read it alone

questions.explanation: Older adults learn best with fewer distractions, more time, and information in smaller chunks. When cognition declines, include family or caregivers in the teaching.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reinforcing teaching for a client who has a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which actions address the cognitive domain of learning? Move the correct actions to the answer box.

options.text: Give the client a pamphlet on carbohydrate counting
options.rationale: Reading materials help the client gain and store knowledge, which is cognitive learning.

options.text: Ask the client questions about which foods raise blood glucose
options.rationale: Question-and-answer is a cognitive teaching method. It checks what the client knows and understands.

options.text: Lead a discussion about the signs of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Discussion builds knowledge of facts the client needs to recognize, which is cognitive learning.

options.text: Have the client return-demonstrate a fingerstick glucose check
options.rationale: Return demonstration shows the client can perform a skill, which is the psychomotor domain.

options.text: Demonstrate how to draw up insulin in a syringe
options.rationale: Demonstrating a hands-on skill teaches the psychomotor domain.

options.text: Role-play how the client will tell friends about the diagnosis
options.rationale: Role play works on feelings, values, and beliefs, which is the affective domain.

questions.summary: Head, heart, hands: cognitive is thinking (lecture, Q&A, discussion), affective is feelings (role play), psychomotor is doing (demonstration, return demonstration).

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to reinforce discharge teaching for a client who has hearing loss. Which actions should the nurse take? Move the correct actions to the answer box.

options.text: Face the client while speaking
options.rationale: Facing the client lets them see your face and lips, which helps them follow what you say.

options.text: Turn off the television in the room
options.rationale: Cutting background noise makes speech easier to hear and keeps the client focused.

options.text: Keep hands away from the face while talking
options.rationale: Hands in front of the mouth block lip movements the client may rely on.

options.text: Raise the voice to a shout
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and makes it harder to understand. Speak clearly at a normal volume.

options.text: Talk faster to keep the session short
options.rationale: Speeding up makes speech harder to follow. Speak clearly and give the client time.

options.text: Teach while the client is eating lunch
options.rationale: Mealtimes are a distraction. Teach in a quiet, low-stimulus setting.

questions.summary: For hearing loss: face to face, speak clearly, cut background noise, hands away from your face.

questions.prompt: During a chart audit, a nurse realizes they consistently spend less time with clients who have limited English proficiency, although the nurse never intended to. The nurse should recognize this as which of the following?

options.text: Explicit bias
Implicit bias
Cultural competence
Etic knowledge

questions.explanation: Implicit bias is unconscious and involuntary and affects perceptions, decisions, and interactions without the person realizing it.

questions.prompt: A nurse tells a coworker, "I'd rather not be assigned to clients of that religion." The charge nurse should recognize this statement as which of the following?

options.text: Explicit bias
Implicit bias
Cultural awareness
Emic knowledge

questions.explanation: Explicit bias is conscious bias from thoughts and beliefs a person is aware of and can report.

questions.prompt: A nurse wants to improve their cultural awareness. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Memorize the health practices of several cultures.
Complete a self-assessment of their own biases.
Ask a family member to interpret for clients.
Review the hospital's policies on visitation.

questions.explanation: Cultural awareness begins with a self-assessment of one's own biases, then investigating and understanding differences between one's own culture and others'.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a client to explain what a family healing ceremony means to them and how it relates to their recovery. The nurse is gaining which type of knowledge?

options.text: Emic knowledge
Etic knowledge
Explicit knowledge
Organizational knowledge

questions.explanation: Emic knowledge is the insider's perspective, defined by members of the culture.

questions.prompt: A nurse reads a research study about health practices common in a particular cultural group. The nurse is gaining which type of knowledge?

options.text: Emic knowledge
Etic knowledge
Implicit knowledge
Personal health literacy

questions.explanation: Etic knowledge is the outsider's perspective, based on external observation, objective data, or scientific theories about a culture.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about cultural competence. Which statement by a student indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "Cultural competence means knowing the definitions of different cultures."
"Cultural competence means integrating nursing care with both emic and etic knowledge."
"Cultural competence means treating every client exactly the same way."
"Cultural competence only matters when a client speaks another language."

questions.explanation: Cultural competence includes appreciating, accepting, and respecting clients' cultural beliefs, open communication and feedback, and integrating nursing care with emic and etic knowledge.

questions.prompt: A nurse cares for two clients from the same cultural background and notices they have very different health practices and beliefs. The nurse should recognize which of the following?

options.text: One of the clients is not following their culture correctly.
Cultural diversity occurs within, as well as among, cultural groups.
Cultural differences only exist between different ethnic groups.
The nurse should base care on the more common practice.

questions.explanation: Cultural diversity occurs within and among cultural groups, so the nurse should never assume all members of a group share the same beliefs.

questions.prompt: A client's name on their insurance card doesn't match the name they give the nurse. Which part of the cultural health assessment is the nurse completing when respectfully clarifying this?

options.text: Demographic assessment
Biological factors
Technological factors
Culture care repatterning

questions.explanation: The demographic assessment lays the foundation for who the client is, and the nurse should be aware that a client's name or gender may differ from their records.
