questions.prompt: A nurse educator is teaching staff how bias can affect client care. Which effects should the educator include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Less compassion shown to certain clients
Less time spent building relationships
Poorer client assessment
Contribution to health care disparities
Improved client outcomes

questions.explanation: Bias can lead to less compassion, less time building relationships, and poorer assessment, which contribute to health care disparities.

questions.prompt: A new urgent care center opens in a rural town. The nurse arranges transportation vouchers for residents who don't have a car. This action is an example of which of the following?

options.text: Health equality
Health equity
Explicit bias
Organizational health literacy

questions.explanation: Equity adjusts for individual needs so everyone can reach the same outcome. Equality gives everyone the same thing, such as simply opening the center to all residents.

questions.prompt: A nurse is beginning care for a newly admitted client from a different cultural background. When should the nurse begin collecting cultural health assessment data?

options.text: At the first encounter with the client
Only if the client requests it
After the client is stabilized for discharge
Only if the client does not speak English

questions.explanation: The cultural health assessment should begin at the first client encounter. The nurse should always ask and never assume.

questions.prompt: A client repeatedly misses follow-up appointments because they have no car and no health insurance. The nurse should recognize these barriers as which of the following?

options.text: Social determinants of health
Implicit bias
Emic knowledge
Culture care preservation

questions.explanation: Social determinants of health are conditions that affect health, quality of life, and well-being and contribute to disparities, such as lack of insurance or transportation.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about health disparities. Which definition should the nurse include?

options.text: Differences in health outcomes between populations, particularly vulnerable groups compared with the majority
The distribution of the same resources to everyone
An individual's ability to understand health information
A blueprint for organizations to improve quality

questions.explanation: Health disparities are differences in health outcomes between populations, particularly vulnerable groups compared with the majority, and can limit access to care.

questions.prompt: A nurse manager is explaining the purpose of the National CLAS standards to staff. Which statement by the manager is accurate?

options.text: "They are a blueprint for organizations to advance health equity, improve quality, and eliminate disparities."
"They are a cultural assessment tool used at the bedside."
"They determine the reading level for all patient materials."
"They describe the three modes of culture care."

questions.explanation: The CLAS standards are a blueprint for health care organizations to advance health equity, improve quality, and eliminate health care disparities.

questions.prompt: After receiving discharge teaching, a client is unable to explain how to take their new medication or why they need it. The nurse should recognize a concern with which of the following?

options.text: Organizational health literacy
Personal health literacy
Health equality
Etic knowledge

questions.explanation: Personal health literacy is the extent to which a person can obtain, process, and understand basic health information.

questions.prompt: A hospital provides simplified health materials in several languages and trains staff to help clients find and use health services. This is an example of which of the following?

options.text: Personal health literacy
Organizational health literacy
Implicit bias
Folk care

questions.explanation: Organizational health literacy is the extent to which organizations equitably help people find, understand, and use health information and services.

questions.prompt: A nurse is creating written education materials for clients. At which reading level should the nurse write the materials?

options.text: College level
12th grade
10th grade
8th grade or lower

questions.explanation: The NIH recommends presenting all health information at an 8th-grade reading level or lower.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing clients on a community health caseload. Which clients should the nurse identify as members of a vulnerable population? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 40-year-old client who is living in poverty
options.rationale: People living in poverty have fewer resources and are a vulnerable population.

options.text: A 91-year-old client who has heart failure
options.rationale: Older adults and people with chronic illness are vulnerable populations.

options.text: A 35-year-old client who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair
options.rationale: People with disabilities face barriers to care and are a vulnerable population.

options.text: A 17-year-old client who is pregnant
options.rationale: Pregnant teens are a vulnerable population.

options.text: A 50-year-old veteran who recently left military service
options.rationale: Veterans are considered a vulnerable population.

questions.explanation: Vulnerable populations face barriers to social, economic, and environmental resources and include people living in poverty, older adults, people with chronic illness or disabilities, pregnant teens, and veterans.

questions.prompt: During an outbreak of influenza, which client should the nurse identify as being at highest risk for infection because of population density?

options.text: A client who lives alone in a rural home
A client who lives in a nursing home
A client who works from home
A client who lives with one roommate in a house

questions.explanation: Living close together, as in nursing homes, shelters, dorms, and apartments, increases the spread of infection.

questions.prompt: A client living in poverty who also experiences racial discrimination and has multiple chronic illnesses reports high stress and recent substance use. The nurse should recognize this as an example of which of the following?

options.text: Intersectionality
Cultural competence
Health equality
Emic knowledge

questions.explanation: Intersectionality is experiencing multiple disparities at the same time, which leads to greater stress, lower self-esteem, and riskier behaviors such as substance use.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing a community emergency plan. Which population should the nurse recognize as disproportionately affected by disasters?

options.text: Young adults
Older adults
Middle-income adults without chronic illness
College students

questions.explanation: Older adults are more vulnerable because of greater physical disabilities and dependence on others, and they are disproportionately affected by disasters.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing barriers that may affect a client's access to health care. Which factors should the nurse assess? Select all that apply.

options.text: Access to transportation
options.rationale: Without transportation, a client may not be able to reach appointments.

options.text: Health insurance
options.rationale: Lack of insurance can keep a client from getting or affording care.

options.text: Geographic location
options.rationale: Living far from services, such as in a rural area, limits access to care.

options.text: Preferred learning style
options.rationale: Learning style affects how teaching is planned, not whether the client can get to care.

options.text: Family history of heart disease
options.rationale: Family history is a health risk factor, not a barrier to accessing care.

questions.explanation: Transportation, health insurance, and geographic location all affect whether a client can reach and pay for care. A preferred learning style shapes how teaching is delivered, and family history is a health risk factor; neither is a barrier to accessing care.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing factors that affect vulnerable populations. Which of the following is a socioeconomic factor?

options.text: Age
English proficiency
Household income
Chronic health conditions

questions.explanation: Socioeconomic factors include education level, employment status, household income, and poverty status. Age and English proficiency are demographic factors, and chronic conditions are health status factors.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing factors that affect vulnerable populations. Which of the following is a health status factor?

options.text: Population density
Health insurance status
Employment status
Household type

questions.explanation: Health status factors include chronic health conditions, disabilities, and health insurance status. Population density and household type are demographic factors, and employment is a socioeconomic factor.

questions.prompt: A transgender client tells the nurse their chosen name and pronouns. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Use the name listed on the client's insurance card.
Use the client's chosen name and pronouns consistently.
Ask the client to provide legal documentation of the name change.
Avoid using the client's name altogether.

questions.explanation: Using a client's chosen name and pronouns shows respect and openness. Inconsistent use is a barrier to gender-affirming care.

questions.prompt: A nurse is explaining Leininger's Theory of Culture Care Diversity and Universality to a group of nursing students. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It guides nurses to give care that fits the client's cultural values, beliefs, and practices."
"It measures how stressful a client perceives their life to be."
"It describes the stages of sleep."
"It is used to determine a client's reading level."

questions.explanation: Leininger's theory, also called Transcultural Nursing Theory, guides nurses to give care that fits the client's cultural values, beliefs, and practices.

questions.prompt: A nurse is using Leininger's Sunrise Enabler. Which of the following is one of its five categories?

options.text: Three modes of care decisions and actions
Twelve cultural domains
Primary and secondary appraisal
Alarm, resistance, and exhaustion

questions.explanation: The five categories are the upper level (worldview), the rays of the sun (basic elements), the central core, the focus on individuals, families, groups, communities, or institutions, and the three modes of care decisions and actions.

questions.prompt: A nurse is completing a cultural assessment based on the basic elements (rays of the sun) of the Sunrise Enabler. Which elements should the nurse assess? Select all that apply.

options.text: Technological factors
Kinship and social factors
Economic factors
Educational factors
Hospital staffing ratios

questions.explanation: The basic elements are technological; religious, spiritual, and philosophical; kinship and social; cultural values, beliefs, and lifeways; biological; political and legal; economic; and educational factors.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a client whether they have access to a phone, internet, or computer. The nurse is assessing which element of the Sunrise Enabler?

options.text: Technological factors
Biological factors
Political and legal factors
Kinship and social factors

questions.explanation: Technological factors include access to a phone, internet, or computer, which affects access to care and communication with providers.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a client about any personal or family history of mental illness or genetic conditions. The nurse is assessing which element of the Sunrise Enabler?

options.text: Biological factors
Economic factors
Educational factors
Technological factors

questions.explanation: Biological factors include personal or family history of physical or mental illness and genetic conditions.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a client, "Who is your support system?" and "What is your marital status?" The nurse is assessing which element of the Sunrise Enabler?

options.text: Kinship and social factors
Technological factors
Political and legal factors
Biological factors

questions.explanation: Kinship and social factors include marital status and support systems such as family and friends.

questions.prompt: A client's grandmother prepares a traditional remedy passed down through generations to help the client recover. The nurse should recognize this as which of the following?

options.text: Folk (generic) care
Integrative care
Culture care repatterning
Etic knowledge

questions.explanation: Folk (generic) care is nonprofessional care based on tradition, given by family or a folk practitioner.

questions.prompt: A client wants to continue using a traditional herbal remedy along with prescribed treatment. The nurse collaborates with the provider so the client can safely use both. The nurse is practicing which of the following?

options.text: Folk care
Integrative care
Explicit bias
Health equality

questions.explanation: In integrative care, the nurse acts as a bridge between folk or naturopathic medicine and Western medicine.

questions.prompt: A client requests a female caregiver because of religious beliefs, and the nurse arranges the assignment. This is an example of which mode of culture care?

options.text: Culture care preservation and maintenance
Culture care accommodation and negotiation
Culture care repatterning and restructuring
Integrative care

questions.explanation: Culture care preservation and maintenance supports the client in maintaining their cultural beliefs and values.

questions.prompt: A client who has diabetes wants to eat traditional holiday foods high in carbohydrates. The nurse helps the client adjust portion sizes so they can still take part safely. This is an example of which mode of culture care?

options.text: Culture care preservation and maintenance
Culture care accommodation and negotiation
Culture care repatterning and restructuring
Folk care

questions.explanation: Culture care accommodation and negotiation helps the client adapt their cultural beliefs and practices for safety, health, and wellness.

questions.prompt: A client's cultural practice is causing harm to their health. The nurse works with the client to change the practice to improve outcomes. This is an example of which mode of culture care?

options.text: Culture care preservation and maintenance
Culture care accommodation and negotiation
Culture care repatterning and restructuring
Emic knowledge

questions.explanation: Culture care repatterning and restructuring helps the client restructure their cultural beliefs to improve health outcomes.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to give discharge instructions to a client who speaks a different language than the nurse. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Consult a certified medical interpreter.
options.rationale: A certified medical interpreter gives accurate translation and protects confidentiality.

options.text: Provide written instructions in the client's preferred language.
options.rationale: Written instructions in the client's language reinforce teaching after discharge.

options.text: Have a family member translate the instructions.
options.rationale: Family members may omit or change information and the client's confidentiality is not protected.

options.text: Ask a staff member who speaks some of the client's language to explain the instructions.
options.rationale: Staff who are not certified interpreters may misinterpret medical information.

options.text: Speak more loudly in English.
options.rationale: Speaking louder does not help a client understand a language they do not speak.

questions.explanation: Discharge teaching with a language barrier requires a certified medical interpreter and written instructions in the client's preferred language. Family members and other staff may misinterpret information and compromise confidentiality.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has hearing loss. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Face the client when speaking.
options.rationale: Facing the client lets them see your face and lips, which helps them follow what you say.

options.text: Reduce background noise.
options.rationale: Less background noise makes speech easier to hear and understand.

options.text: Use a loud tone of voice.
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and does not make words clearer.

options.text: Speak at a faster pace.
options.rationale: Speaking faster makes words harder to follow; speak clearly at a normal pace.

options.text: Write everything down on paper.
options.rationale: Writing down key information can help, but writing everything replaces conversation instead of supporting it.

questions.explanation: The nurse should face the client and reduce background noise. A loud voice, faster speech, or writing everything down are not effective strategies.

questions.prompt: A nurse is admitting a client who speaks limited English. Which actions should the nurse take? Move the correct actions to the answer box.

options.text: Request a certified medical interpreter
options.rationale: A certified medical interpreter gives accurate, confidential interpretation.

options.text: Provide written instructions in the client's language
options.rationale: Written instructions in the client's language back up what was said.

options.text: Respectfully ask how the client prefers to be addressed
options.rationale: Name or gender may differ from records, so ask respectfully at the first encounter.

options.text: Ask the client's adult daughter to interpret
options.rationale: Family can leave out or change information and breaks confidentiality.

options.text: Ask a bilingual staff member from another unit to interpret
options.rationale: Other staff aren't certified interpreters and can omit or alter information.

options.text: Raise your voice so the client understands
options.rationale: Speaking louder doesn't fix a language barrier.

questions.summary: Always a certified medical interpreter, never family or other staff.

questions.prompt: A nurse is using Leininger's three modes of care. Which actions are examples of cultural care accommodation and negotiation? Move the correct actions to the answer box.

options.text: Offer smaller portions of traditional holiday foods to a client who has diabetes
options.rationale: The practice is adapted so it stays safe, which is accommodation and negotiation.

options.text: Work with a client to plan medication times around religious fasting hours
options.rationale: The care plan is adjusted to fit the practice safely, which is accommodation and negotiation.

options.text: Arrange a female caregiver as the client requested
options.rationale: Honoring the request as-is is preservation and maintenance.

options.text: Help a client replace a home practice that is harming their health
options.rationale: Changing a harmful practice is repatterning and restructuring.

options.text: Support the client in keeping a daily prayer routine unchanged
options.rationale: Keeping a practice as-is is preservation and maintenance.

questions.summary: PAR: Preservation keeps it, Accommodation adapts it, Repatterning changes it.

questions.prompt: A nurse is talking with a 17-year-old client who says, "My parents are both pharmacists, so I'm going to pharmacy school. I've never really thought about doing anything else." Which identity status should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Identity achievement
Moratorium
Foreclosure
Identity diffusion

questions.explanation: Foreclosure is commitment without exploration, adopting the expectations of authority figures without questioning them. Achievement requires exploring first; moratorium is exploring without committing; diffusion is neither.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client's self-concept. Which question should the nurse ask to assess role performance?

options.text: "How would you describe yourself?"
"How successful do you feel in fulfilling your responsibilities as a parent?"
"How do you respond when you experience failure?"
"Which aspects of your appearance would you like to change?"

questions.explanation: Asking how successful the client feels in their roles assesses role performance. Self-description assesses identity, response to failure assesses self-esteem, and appearance assesses body image.

questions.prompt: A client works full time, cares for her father who has dementia, and is raising three children. She tells the nurse, "There aren't enough hours in the day to do everything that's expected of me." Which role stressor is the client experiencing?

options.text: Role ambiguity
Role overload
Role clarity
Role enhancement

questions.explanation: Role overload occurs when the demands of multiple roles exceed a person's ability to manage them. Role ambiguity is unclear expectations; role clarity and role enhancement reduce stress.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client for behaviors that may indicate an altered self-concept. Which findings should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tearfulness during the interview
Frequently apologizing to the nurse
Difficulty making simple decisions
Asking questions about the treatment plan
Referring to themself as "useless"

questions.explanation: Tearfulness, being overly apologetic, indecisiveness, and negative self-talk can indicate an altered self-concept. Asking questions about treatment shows engagement in care.

questions.prompt: A nurse is planning care for a client who had a below-the-knee amputation and is unable to return to work. Which actions should the nurse include to promote a healthy self-concept? Select all that apply.

options.text: Encourage the client to express feelings about the change in body function.
Discuss available rehabilitation and support resources.
Perform all ADLs for the client to conserve their energy.
Establish goals collaboratively with the client and family.
Postpone addressing emotional needs until physical rehabilitation is complete.

questions.explanation: Expressing feelings, using resources, and collaborative goal-setting support adaptation and a client-centered plan. Doing all ADLs promotes dependence, and delaying emotional care ignores the holistic approach.

questions.prompt: A nurse manager is discussing emotional intelligence with staff. Which statement by a staff nurse shows an understanding of self-regulation?

options.text: "I take a few deep breaths before I respond when a family member yells at me."
"I can usually tell when a coworker is upset."
"I stay persistent when working toward my goals."
"I find it easy to build rapport with new clients."

questions.explanation: Self-regulation is managing one's emotional state, or thinking before acting. Sensing a coworker's feelings is empathy, persistence toward goals is motivation, and building rapport is social skill.

questions.prompt: A school nurse is planning a health education program on body image. Which age group should the nurse recognize as most vulnerable to body dissatisfaction?

options.text: School-age children
Adolescents
Middle adults
Older adults

questions.explanation: Adolescents are the most vulnerable because rapid physical and hormonal changes during puberty coincide with greater exposure to cultural ideals of attractiveness.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which client statement shows low self-efficacy?

options.text: "I'm nervous, but I know I can learn to check my blood sugar."
"I'll never be able to manage all of this, so why even try?"
"Can you show me the insulin injection one more time?"
"My daughter and I are going to take the diabetes class together."

questions.explanation: Low self-efficacy shows up as self-doubt and giving up before trying. The other statements show confidence, engagement in learning, and use of support.

questions.prompt: A 19-year-old client tells the nurse, "I keep switching my major between nursing, art, and business. I get so anxious because I can't decide what I want to do with my life." Which identity status should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Identity achievement
Moratorium
Foreclosure
Identity diffusion

questions.explanation: Moratorium is active exploration without commitment, often with anxiety and feeling overwhelmed. Achievement requires both exploring and committing; foreclosure is commitment without exploring; diffusion lacks both.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing the health histories of several clients. Which clients should the nurse identify as experiencing self-esteem stressors? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client who recently retired and says, "I feel like I have no purpose now."
A client whose spouse died 6 months ago
A client who was laid off from their job last month
A client who was recently promoted at work
A client who just completed their first marathon

questions.explanation: Self-esteem stressors include feeling irrelevant after retirement, loss of social support after a spouse's death, and loss of career. A promotion and completing a marathon are more likely to boost self-esteem.

questions.prompt: A client tells the nurse, "My manager wants me to work this Saturday, but that's my son's championship game and I promised him I'd be there." The nurse should recognize the client is experiencing which of the following?

options.text: Role ambiguity
Role conflict
Role clarity
Identity confusion

questions.explanation: Role conflict happens when two or more role expectations (employee and parent) can't be met at the same time. Role ambiguity is unclear expectations; role clarity reduces stress; identity confusion is an unclear sense of self.

questions.prompt: A client says, "I've always wanted to be a strong leader, but I never speak up in meetings at work. I feel like such a failure." Which concept should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Self-concept congruence
Self-concept incongruence
Self-actualization
High self-efficacy

questions.explanation: Incongruence occurs when the ideal self doesn't match actual life experiences, leading to negative feelings and uncertainty. Congruence and self-actualization require alignment.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about ways to enhance self-awareness. Which strategies should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep a reflection journal.
Ask peers and instructors for feedback.
Complete self-assessments.
Avoid considering other people's points of view.
Practice listening carefully to understand others.

questions.explanation: Journaling, asking for feedback, self-assessments, and careful listening all build self-awareness. Seeking to understand other points of view is also recommended because it helps a person see situations the way others do.

questions.prompt: A client who recently lost their job tells the nurse, "I feel worthless." Which question should the nurse ask to assess the client's self-esteem?

options.text: "What words might others use to describe you?"
"What are some accomplishments or qualities that make you feel good about yourself?"
"How would you describe your physical appearance?"
"What kind of support do you have to fulfill your roles?"

questions.explanation: Asking about accomplishments and qualities assesses self-esteem. How others would describe the client assesses identity, physical appearance assesses body image, and support for roles assesses role performance.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client from a cultural background different from the nurse's own. Which action shows the nurse understands culture's influence on self-concept?

options.text: Assume the client shares the same beliefs as others from their ethnic group.
Ask the client about their personal cultural beliefs and practices.
Base the plan of care on common traits of the client's culture.
Encourage the client to adopt the values of the dominant culture.

questions.explanation: Differences exist within cultures and even within families, so the nurse should ask about the client's own beliefs. Assuming shared beliefs or relying on general traits leads to stereotyping.

questions.prompt: A client who recently divorced tells the nurse, "I was married for 20 years. I don't even know who I am anymore." The nurse should recognize the client is experiencing which of the following?

options.text: Identity confusion
Role overload
Body image disturbance
Identity foreclosure

questions.explanation: Divorce is an identity stressor, and trouble adapting to it can cause identity confusion, an unclear sense of self. Role overload means too many demands; foreclosure is an identity status.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing a class about factors that influence body image across the lifespan. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hormonal changes during puberty can affect body image.
options.rationale: Puberty brings rapid body changes, and adolescents are especially vulnerable to body image concerns.

options.text: Weight stigma can negatively affect a person's self-concept.
options.rationale: Negative social attitudes about weight can harm body image and self-esteem.

options.text: Age-related loss of muscle and bone mass seldom affects how older adults see their bodies.
options.rationale: Aging changes such as loss of muscle and bone mass can lead older adults to reevaluate their body image.

options.text: Body image becomes fixed once a person reaches adulthood.
options.rationale: Body image continues to change throughout life.

options.text: In adults, body image is affected only by visible changes such as scars.
options.rationale: Conditions that are not visible, such as diabetes, can also affect body image.

questions.explanation: Puberty and weight stigma both affect body image. Body image keeps changing through adulthood, aging changes such as loss of muscle and bone mass can affect it, and changes that are not visible, such as diabetes, can affect it too.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has low self-esteem after a stroke left them with right-sided weakness. Which intervention should the nurse implement?

options.text: Help the client identify past accomplishments and strengths.
Discourage the client from talking about the losses they've experienced.
Tell the client, "Don't worry, you'll be back to normal in no time."
Make daily care decisions for the client to reduce their stress.

questions.explanation: Identifying past and current accomplishments promotes a positive self-concept. Discouraging expression of feelings blocks coping, false reassurance is nontherapeutic, and making decisions for the client promotes dependence.

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old client tells the nurse, "I shadowed a nurse, a respiratory therapist, and a physical therapist before choosing nursing. I just enrolled in my first nursing course." Which identity status should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Identity achievement
Moratorium
Foreclosure
Identity diffusion

questions.explanation: Identity achievement is exploring alternatives and then committing. Moratorium lacks commitment, foreclosure lacks exploration, and diffusion lacks both.

questions.prompt: A 20-year-old client spends most days playing online games and says, "I don't really care what I do with my life. I'll figure it out eventually." Which identity status should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Identity achievement
Moratorium
Foreclosure
Identity diffusion

questions.explanation: Identity diffusion is a lack of both exploration and commitment; the person drifts without purpose or direction. Moratorium involves active exploration, often with anxiety.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of parents about identity formation. Which statement by a parent indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "My teen's identity will be set by the time they turn 18."
"Identity keeps developing throughout adulthood, but it's most intense during adolescence."
"If my teen tries out different identities, it means something is wrong."
"Identity formation is mostly finished by early childhood."

questions.explanation: Identity formation is lifelong, but it is most intense during adolescence. Trying out different roles and identities is an expected part of adolescent development.

questions.prompt: A newly hired nurse tells a coworker, "Nobody has explained what I'm responsible for on this unit, and I'm not sure what's expected of me." Which role stressor is the nurse experiencing?

options.text: Role conflict
Role ambiguity
Role overload
Role satisfaction

questions.explanation: Role ambiguity is a lack of clarity about what is expected, which leads to doubt and lower commitment. Role conflict is competing expectations, and role overload is too many demands.

questions.prompt: A client caring for a spouse who has advanced Parkinson's disease tells the nurse, "I can't keep up with all of his care needs. I feel like I'm failing as his caregiver." The nurse should recognize the client is experiencing which of the following?

options.text: Role strain
Role clarity
Role enhancement
Identity foreclosure

questions.explanation: Role strain is difficulty meeting the responsibilities of a particular life role. Role clarity and role enhancement reduce stress, and foreclosure is an identity status.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client who reports stress related to their various life roles. Which role performance stressors should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Role conflict
options.rationale: Role conflict occurs when two role expectations cannot both be met at the same time.

options.text: Role overload
options.rationale: Role overload occurs when a person has too many roles at once.

options.text: Role modeling
options.rationale: Role modeling is learning behaviors by watching others, not a role stressor.

options.text: Role satisfaction
options.rationale: Role satisfaction is a positive result of meeting role expectations, not a stressor.

options.text: Role enhancement
options.rationale: Role enhancement describes a role adding to well-being, not causing stress.

questions.explanation: Role conflict and role overload are role performance stressors, along with role strain and role ambiguity. Role modeling, role satisfaction, and role enhancement do not cause role stress.

questions.prompt: An adolescent client tells the nurse they feel distressed because their gender identity does not match the sex they were assigned at birth. The nurse should recognize this as which of the following?

options.text: Gender dysphoria
Identity diffusion
Role ambiguity
Self-concept congruence

questions.explanation: Gender dysphoria is a feeling of incongruity between one's gender identity and assigned sex at birth, and it is an identity stressor that can threaten self-concept.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client who has psoriasis on the face and arms. Which question should the nurse ask to assess the client's body image?

options.text: "How comfortable are you expressing your opinions?"
"Which aspects of your physical appearance do you like and appreciate?"
"How would others describe you?"
"How do you cope when your roles conflict?"

questions.explanation: Questions about physical appearance assess body image. Expressing opinions assesses self-esteem, how others describe the client assesses identity, and coping with conflicting roles assesses role performance.

questions.prompt: A nurse is completing a self-concept assessment. Which question should the nurse ask to assess the client's identity?

options.text: "How is your identity influenced by others or by society?"
"How important is it to always look your best?"
"How much do you worry about what others think of you?"
"Describe two or three of your primary roles."

questions.explanation: Asking how identity is influenced by others or society assesses identity. Looking your best assesses body image, worrying about others' opinions assesses self-esteem, and primary roles assess role performance.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for several clients who recently had a colostomy placed. Which client requires further assessment for negative self-esteem related to body image?

options.text: A client who asks about local ostomy support groups
A client who refuses to look at the stoma and asks family not to visit
A client who asks for help choosing clothing that fits over the pouch
A client who practices changing the pouch with the nurse

questions.explanation: Refusing to look at the stoma and withdrawing from family suggest negative self-esteem related to body image. The other clients are coping by seeking support and learning self-care.

questions.prompt: A nurse is planning interventions to improve self-efficacy for a client after a percutaneous coronary intervention. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Provide ongoing education.
Offer emotional support.
Involve the client's family in care.
Encourage participation in group activities.
Discourage the client from asking questions about their recovery.

questions.explanation: Self-efficacy interventions include ongoing education, emotional support, family involvement, and group activities to build competence and social support. Discouraging questions would undermine the client's confidence and learning.

questions.prompt: A client tells the nurse, "I'm a very patient person." The client's family later describes the client as short-tempered. The nurse should recognize this reflects which component of self-concept?

options.text: Self-image
Ideal self
Self-efficacy
Role performance

questions.explanation: Self-image is how a person views their own qualities, and it may not be consistent with reality or with how others see them.

questions.prompt: A nursing student says, "Someday I want to be a respected, dependable nurse that clients trust." This statement reflects which component of self-concept?

options.text: Self-image
Self-esteem
Ideal self
Identity confusion

questions.explanation: The ideal self is what a person desires to be, such as strong, intelligent, respected, and appreciated.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client the night before surgery. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates the emotional intelligence domain of empathy?

options.text: The nurse recognizes the client's fear and adjusts their approach to address the client's concerns.
The nurse stays calm when the surgical schedule changes unexpectedly.
The nurse sets a goal to become certified in perioperative nursing.
The nurse reflects on their own strengths and weaknesses after the shift.

questions.explanation: Empathy is understanding others' emotions, needs, and concerns and using that knowledge to guide behavior. Staying calm is self-regulation, setting career goals is motivation, and reflecting on strengths is self-awareness.

questions.prompt: A nurse observes that a client appears disheveled, is tearful, and repeatedly says, "I'm sorry for being such a burden." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Refer the client to a support group.
Use open-ended questions to explore the client's feelings.
Tell the client there is no need to apologize.
Assist the client with hygiene and grooming.

questions.explanation: Assessment comes first. These behaviors may indicate an altered self-concept, so the nurse should use therapeutic communication to explore the client's feelings before planning interventions. Telling the client not to apologize dismisses their feelings.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing an adolescent client who has a distorted body image related to pressure to be thin. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Tell the client their weight is normal and there's nothing to worry about.
Focus the assessment only on the client's height and weight.
Involve significant others to gain insight into how the client is perceived by others.
Avoid discussing messages the client receives from friends and social media.

questions.explanation: Involving significant others during assessment helps the nurse understand how the client is perceived by others. The nurse should also explore the impact of messages from family, friends, and media. False reassurance and a purely physical focus are not therapeutic.

questions.prompt: A nurse is evaluating a client's progress after an amputation. Which findings indicate the plan of care for altered self-concept has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client verbalizes statements of self-worth.
options.rationale: Statements of self-worth show improving self-esteem.

options.text: The client uses healthy coping strategies during physical therapy.
options.rationale: Healthy coping shows the client is adapting to the change in body function.

options.text: The client keeps the residual limb covered and asks staff to do all dressing changes.
options.rationale: Avoiding the residual limb suggests the client has not yet accepted the change in body image.

options.text: The client refuses to discuss being fitted for a prosthesis.
options.rationale: Refusing to discuss a prosthesis is avoidance, which signals an unresolved concern.

options.text: The client states, "I'm useless now."
options.rationale: Negative self-talk shows low self-esteem that still needs to be addressed.

questions.explanation: Statements of self-worth and healthy coping show the plan is working. Avoiding the residual limb, refusing to discuss a prosthesis, and negative self-talk show unresolved self-concept concerns.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing how a client's culture influences their self-concept. Which client statement reflects a healthy integration of culture?

options.text: "My family's traditions help me feel confident in who I am."
"I try to hide my cultural background so I fit in."
"I compare myself to people on social media to decide how I should look."
"My culture doesn't really matter to how I see myself."

questions.explanation: Individuals who have effectively integrated their culture tend to have a healthier self-concept, and it protects them against biases and stereotypes projected by media.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about self-concept. Which statement by a student indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "Self-concept is fixed once it forms in early childhood."
"Self-concept can change based on new experiences and feedback."
"Self-concept affects a person's thoughts but not their behavior."
"Self-concept is determined mostly by genetics."

questions.explanation: Self-concept is learned and dynamic, and people refine it based on new information and feedback. It influences behavior, choices, and interactions with others, not just internal thoughts.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a 14-year-old male client who has not yet gone through a growth spurt and is shorter than his peers. Which of the following should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Boys who mature later report greater body dissatisfaction than early-maturing peers.
Adolescent males rarely have body image concerns.
Body image concerns in adolescence are limited to females.
Late maturation improves body image because it delays societal pressure.

questions.explanation: Boys who mature later and have not achieved socially accepted body ideals report greater body dissatisfaction than peers who mature earlier. Adolescent males are not immune to body image concerns.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing clients for role stressors. Which statements describe a role stressor? Move the correct statements to the answer box.

options.text: "My boss wants me to work Saturday, but that's my son's championship game."
options.rationale: Role conflict: two role expectations at the same time.

options.text: "Between work, school, and caring for my mom, I have too many roles."
options.rationale: Role overload: too many roles at once.

options.text: "No one has told me what I'm supposed to be doing in my new job."
options.rationale: Role ambiguity: no idea what's expected.

options.text: "I can't keep up with everything my job demands."
options.rationale: Role strain: can't meet one role's demands.

options.text: "I finally understand what is expected of me at work."
options.rationale: Role clarity isn't a stressor.

options.text: "Becoming a grandparent has made my life richer."
options.rationale: Role enhancement isn't a stressor.

options.text: "I really enjoy being a parent."
options.rationale: Role satisfaction isn't a stressor.

questions.summary: Too many roles will SOAC you: strain, overload, ambiguity, conflict.

questions.prompt: A nurse is evaluating a client who had a mastectomy 1 week ago. Which findings indicate the client is adapting to the change in body image? Move the correct findings to the answer box.

options.text: Looks at the incision during a dressing change
options.rationale: Looking at the change shows the client is starting to accept their body image.

options.text: States, "I'm learning to accept how my body looks now."
options.rationale: Verbalizing self-acceptance shows care is working.

options.text: Asks about a support group for breast cancer survivors
options.rationale: Seeking support is healthy coping.

options.text: Refuses visitors
options.rationale: Withdrawing is a sign of negative self-esteem after a body change.

options.text: Keeps their eyes closed during dressing changes
options.rationale: Avoiding the body change means the client isn't adapting yet.

options.text: Apologizes repeatedly to the nurse
options.rationale: Over-apologizing is a red flag for low self-esteem.

questions.summary: It worked if the client verbalizes self-acceptance, accepts the body change, and uses healthy coping.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who asks about using melatonin for sleep. Which statement by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "Melatonin is non-habit forming and has few adverse effects."
"Melatonin is the most commonly prescribed sleep medication."
"Melatonin works better than any other sleep medication."
"Melatonin should only be used by older adults."

questions.explanation: Melatonin is cost-effective, non-habit forming, and has few adverse effects, and it may be first-line for all ages. However, its effectiveness may be limited, and nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics are the most commonly prescribed sleep meds.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for an older adult client who reports difficulty sleeping. The provider wants to start with the option that has the fewest adverse effects and no risk of dependence. Which medication should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Lorazepam
Zolpidem
Melatonin
Diphenhydramine

questions.explanation: Melatonin may be the first-line option for all ages because it is non-habit forming with few adverse effects. Benzodiazepines carry dependence risk and require caution in older adults, zolpidem has abuse potential, and diphenhydramine causes anticholinergic effects.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing sleep medications with a group of nursing students. Which class of medications should the nurse identify as the most commonly prescribed for sleep?

options.text: Benzodiazepines
Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics
Antihistamines
Antidepressants

questions.explanation: Nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics (the z-drugs, such as zolpidem) are the most commonly prescribed sleep medications.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for zolpidem. The nurse should instruct the client that which of the following is an adverse effect of this medication?

options.text: Urinary retention
Memory loss
Hypertension
Bradycardia

questions.explanation: Adverse effects of nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics include GI discomfort, hallucinations, and memory loss. Urinary retention is associated with OTC antihistamine sleep aids.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who plans to use diphenhydramine for sleep. Which adverse effects should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dry mouth
Difficulty urinating
Constipation
Visual disturbances
Diarrhea

questions.explanation: OTC sleep aids such as diphenhydramine can cause daytime drowsiness, dry mouth, visual disturbances, difficulty urinating, and constipation. The nurse should encourage the client to discuss options with their provider first.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing a prescription for lorazepam for an 82-year-old client who has insomnia. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report to the provider?

options.text: The client drinks one cup of decaf coffee each morning.
The client has decreased kidney and liver function.
The client naps for 20 minutes each afternoon.
The client reports mild anxiety about sleeping.

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines should be used cautiously in older adults with decreased liver and kidney function because the medication may not be cleared effectively.

questions.prompt: A client who has been taking clonazepam for sleep asks why the provider wants to stop it after a few weeks. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "It stops working after a few weeks."
"Long-term use can lead to physical dependence."
"It causes high blood pressure over time."
"It is only approved for use in children."

questions.explanation: Clients can develop physical dependence on benzodiazepines, so they are not recommended for long-term use.

questions.prompt: A hospitalized client asks the nurse for a snack before bed. Which snack should the nurse offer to promote sleep?

options.text: A piece of candy
Toast with peanut butter
Slices of lunchmeat
A cup of cheese cubes

questions.explanation: A bedtime snack that promotes sleep pairs a carbohydrate with a protein. Protein alone (lunchmeat, cheese) is not recommended, and candy is a simple sugar with no protein.

questions.prompt: A nurse wakes a client at 0200 to obtain vital signs. The client is confused and groggy for the next 45 minutes. The nurse should recognize that the client was most likely awakened from which stage of sleep?

options.text: Wake stage
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3

questions.explanation: Stage 3 is the deepest sleep. A person awakened during stage 3 may have mental cloudiness that lasts 30 to 60 minutes.

questions.prompt: A nurse observes a sleeping client whose eyes are moving rapidly under the eyelids, whose breathing is irregular, and whose heart rate is slightly elevated. The client's limbs are completely relaxed. Which stage of sleep is the client in?

options.text: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
REM

questions.explanation: During REM (stage 4), breathing is irregular, heart rate may be elevated, and skeletal muscles are atonic. It is the dreaming stage.

questions.prompt: A nursing student asks why the body loses skeletal muscle tone during REM sleep. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "It lowers the heart rate to its slowest point."
"It prevents the person from physically acting out their dreams."
"It allows muscles to repair and regenerate."
"It helps the person fall into deeper sleep."

questions.explanation: Skeletal muscles are atonic during REM, which protects the person from acting out their dreams. Muscle and tissue repair occurs in stage 3.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client recovering from major surgery. The nurse explains the importance of deep sleep. Which process should the nurse identify as occurring during stage 3 sleep?

options.text: Dreaming
Repair and regeneration of muscles, tissues, and bones
Increased heart rate and irregular breathing
Alpha wave activity

questions.explanation: During stage 3, the immune system strengthens and muscles, tissues, and bones repair and regenerate. Pulse and respirations are at their lowest. Dreaming and irregular breathing occur during REM.

questions.prompt: A nurse educator is teaching newly hired nurses about expected age-related changes in sleep before they care for older adult clients. Which changes should the educator include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decreased stage 3 sleep
options.rationale: Older adults spend less time in stage 3, the deepest sleep.

options.text: Waking more frequently during the night
options.rationale: Older adults wake more often during the night.

options.text: Taking longer to fall asleep
options.rationale: It takes older adults longer to fall asleep.

options.text: Needing only about 4 to 5 hours of sleep each night
options.rationale: Older adults are still recommended to get 7 to 8 hours of sleep.

options.text: More REM (rapid eye movement) cycles than younger adults
options.rationale: Older adults have fewer REM cycles, not more.

questions.explanation: Older adults have less stage 3 sleep, wake more often, and take longer to fall asleep. They have fewer REM (rapid eye movement) cycles, not more, and are still recommended to get 7 to 8 hours of sleep.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a class about the physiology of sleep. The nurse should include that which of the following occurs as a result of sleep?

options.text: Decreased ability to concentrate
Weakened immune system
Transfer of memory from short-term to long-term
Increased cortisol release

questions.explanation: During sleep, the thalamus and cerebral cortex process information and transfer it from short-term to long-term memory. Sleep also strengthens the immune system and lowers cortisol release.

questions.prompt: A nurse is explaining the circadian rhythm to a client. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It only works when there are environmental cues like light."
"It recurs about every 24 hours and syncs with cues such as light and temperature."
"It is controlled entirely by the amount of caffeine you drink."
"It resets every 8 hours."

questions.explanation: The circadian rhythm controls the sleep–wake cycle about every 24 hours and synchronizes with environmental cues like light and temperature, although the body can maintain it without prompts.

questions.prompt: A client tells the nurse, "I stayed up all night studying, and the next night I slept deeper than usual." The nurse should recognize this is due to which of the following?

options.text: Circadian rhythm
Sleep–wake homeostasis
Sensory overload
Selective sleep deprivation

questions.explanation: Sleep–wake homeostasis helps the body remember to sleep after a given time, and sleep deepens according to the amount of sleep deprivation the person has experienced.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about the effects of sleep deprivation. Which effects should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Impaired judgment and decreased response time
options.rationale: Lack of sleep slows reaction time and impairs judgment, raising accident risk.

options.text: Increased risk for depression
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation is linked to a higher risk of depression.

options.text: Improved blood glucose control in clients who have type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation worsens blood glucose control in type 2 diabetes.

options.text: Reduced risk of migraines
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation can trigger migraines rather than prevent them.

options.text: Permanent memory loss after a single sleepless night
options.rationale: One lost night can affect concentration the next day, but it does not cause permanent memory loss.

questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation impairs judgment and response time and increases the risk of depression. It worsens, not improves, glucose control in type 2 diabetes, can trigger migraines, and one sleepless night does not cause permanent memory loss.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client in the intensive care unit. Which actions should the nurse take to reduce the risk of sensory overload? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dim the lights at night.
options.rationale: Lower light reduces stimulation and supports the sleep cycle.

options.text: Offer earplugs and an eye mask.
options.rationale: Earplugs and an eye mask block noise and light that contribute to sensory overload.

options.text: Schedule each care activity at a separate time through the night so each one is brief.
options.rationale: Spreading care out causes more interruptions; clustering care reduces them.

options.text: Obtain vital signs every hour throughout the night regardless of the client's condition.
options.rationale: Vital signs that are not needed interrupt sleep and add stimulation.

options.text: Leave the television on overnight for background noise.
options.rationale: Television noise and light add to sensory overload.

questions.explanation: Dimming the lights and offering earplugs and an eye mask lower stimulation. Spreading care across the night, hourly vital signs that are not needed, and an overnight television add interruptions and stimulation; care should be clustered instead.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about sleep hygiene. Which statement by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I'll sleep in on the weekends to catch up on rest."
"I'll stop drinking coffee at least 6 hours before bedtime."
"I'll watch TV in bed until I fall asleep."
"I'll work out right before bed to tire myself out."

questions.explanation: Stimulants like caffeine should be avoided 4 to 6 hours before bedtime. A consistent sleep schedule, keeping electronics out of the bedroom, and avoiding exercise close to bedtime also promote sleep.

questions.prompt: A client reports lying awake in bed for over an hour most nights. Which instruction should the nurse provide?

options.text: "Stay in bed with your eyes closed until you fall asleep."
"Get up, go to another room, and do a quiet activity until you feel tired."
"Take a longer nap during the day to make up for lost sleep."
"Watch TV in bed to help you relax."

questions.explanation: If a client can't fall asleep, they should get up, go to another room, and do a quiet activity like reading or listening to music, then return when tired. Staying in bed while restless contributes to sleep deprivation.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing a client's sleep diary. Which behaviors should the nurse identify as contributing to sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stays in bed when unable to sleep
Sleeps 3 hours later on weekends
Keeps a television in the bedroom
Takes a warm shower before bed
Keeps the bedroom dark and cool

questions.explanation: Staying in bed while restless, changing sleep patterns on weekends, and keeping electronics in the bedroom contribute to sleep deprivation. A bedtime routine and a dark, cool room promote sleep.

questions.prompt: A nurse who works rotating night shifts asks about health risks. Which response by the occupational health nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Night-shift work has no long-term health effects."
"Night-shift workers have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, obesity, and diabetes."
"Night-shift work improves circadian rhythm over time."
"Night-shift workers are less likely to experience daytime sleepiness."

questions.explanation: Shift workers have a disrupted circadian rhythm, excessive daytime sleepiness, and a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease, obesity, and diabetes.

questions.prompt: An adolescent client tells the nurse they use their phone in bed until they fall asleep. Which effect should the nurse include when teaching the client?

options.text: Longer total sleep time
Improved sleep quality
Increased daytime sleepiness
Decreased risk of depression

questions.explanation: Using a cell phone after going to bed is associated with shorter sleep duration, poor sleep quality, and daytime sleepiness, and it is a risk factor for depression.

questions.prompt: A client reports difficulty falling asleep and waking at 0400 every morning unable to return to sleep, even though they go to bed with plenty of time to rest. Which sleep disorder should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Narcolepsy
Insomnia
Hypersomnia
Central sleep apnea

questions.explanation: Insomnia is an ongoing inability to sleep despite the opportunity, including trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking early.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who is suspected of having obstructive sleep apnea. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Polysomnography
Electrocardiogram
Electroencephalogram alone
Pulmonary function test

questions.explanation: OSA is diagnosed with polysomnography, usually in a sleep lab. It records heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, oxygen saturation, brain waves, body movements, and snoring.

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old client reports working overtime at a high-stress job, recently gaining 10 lb, and starting to smoke again. The client's partner says the snoring is "out of control," and the client feels exhausted all day. Which sleep disorder should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Narcolepsy
Restless legs syndrome
Obstructive sleep apnea
Night terrors

questions.explanation: Snoring, obesity, smoking, and daytime exhaustion are consistent with OSA, which involves recurrent upper airway collapse during sleep.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has obstructive sleep apnea. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear the CPAP device while sleeping.
options.rationale: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) keeps the airway open during sleep.

options.text: Follow a healthy weight-loss program.
options.rationale: Weight loss reduces tissue around the airway that contributes to collapse.

options.text: Avoid alcohol.
options.rationale: Alcohol relaxes the airway muscles and worsens obstruction.

options.text: Take a sedative at bedtime to sleep more deeply.
options.rationale: Sedatives relax the airway muscles and can make apnea episodes worse.

options.text: Sleep on your back.
options.rationale: Lying on the back lets the airway collapse more easily and can worsen OSA.

questions.explanation: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), weight loss, and avoiding alcohol are key parts of treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), along with not smoking. Sedatives relax the airway muscles, and sleeping on the back lets the airway collapse more easily.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing the health histories of several clients. Which client is at highest risk for central sleep apnea?

options.text: A client who has enlarged tonsils
A client who has heart failure
A client who has obesity
A client who has iron deficiency

questions.explanation: Central sleep apnea is a reduction in the brain's signals to the respiratory muscles. Common causes are heart failure and opioid overdose. Enlarged tonsils and obesity are associated with obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.prompt: In which of the following sleep disorders does the client experience sudden, uncontrollable episodes of sleep?

options.text: Insomnia
Obstructive sleep apnea
Narcolepsy
Restless legs syndrome

questions.explanation: Narcolepsy is characterized by sudden sleepiness and sudden periods of sleep. Clients have difficulty staying awake.

questions.prompt: A client who has narcolepsy suddenly loses muscle tone and slumps over while laughing at a joke. The nurse should document this as which of the following?

options.text: Cataplexy
Seizure
Sleep paralysis
Hypopnea

questions.explanation: Cataplexy is a brief loss of voluntary muscle tone triggered by an emotional stimulus, such as laughter. It occurs in narcolepsy type 1.

questions.prompt: A client reports sleeping 10 hours every night but still feeling exhausted throughout the day. The client's circadian rhythm is normal. Which sleep disorder should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Insomnia
Hypersomnia
Central sleep apnea
Night terrors

questions.explanation: Hypersomnia is excessive daytime fatigue that does not improve with more sleep and is not caused by poor nighttime sleep or a disturbed circadian rhythm.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client who has restless legs syndrome. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "Drink a cup of coffee in the evening to reduce symptoms."
"Avoid caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol."
"Your symptoms will be worse in the morning."
"Lying still in bed will relieve the sensations."

questions.explanation: Avoiding caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol may help control RLS. Symptoms worsen in the evening and with inactivity, such as lying down to sleep.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client who reports trouble sleeping. Which finding is consistent with restless legs syndrome?

options.text: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing
An uncomfortable urge to move the legs that worsens when lying down at night
Sudden loss of muscle tone when laughing
Waking in panic with no memory of the event

questions.explanation: RLS is an uncontrollable urge to move the legs with an uncomfortable sensation, worsening in the evening and with inactivity. It can be associated with iron or vitamin deficiencies.

questions.prompt: A parent tells the nurse their 5-year-old child screams and seems terrified shortly after falling asleep but doesn't remember it the next morning. Which information about night terrors should the nurse include when teaching the parent?

options.text: "They usually happen within the first few hours after your child falls asleep."
"They usually happen in the early morning hours, right before your child wakes up."
"Your child will usually remember the frightening dream in detail."
"Night terrors are more common in adults than in children."

questions.explanation: Night terrors occur during NREM sleep in the first third of the night, the person has no memory of them, and they are most common in young children. Early-morning episodes that the person remembers describe nightmares, which occur during REM sleep in the second half of the night.

questions.prompt: A child wakes early in the morning crying and describes a scary dream about being chased. The nurse should recognize this as which of the following?

options.text: A night terror occurring during NREM sleep
A nightmare occurring during REM sleep
Cataplexy
Sensory overload

questions.explanation: Nightmares occur during REM sleep, most commonly in the second half of the night, and the person remembers the dream. Night terrors occur during NREM sleep in the first third of the night with no recall.

questions.prompt: A nurse is planning nonpharmacological interventions to promote sleep for a hospitalized client. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Guided imagery
options.rationale: Guided imagery relaxes the client and helps them fall asleep.

options.text: Music therapy
options.rationale: Soft music promotes relaxation before sleep.

options.text: Massage
options.rationale: Massage relaxes muscles and helps the client settle for sleep.

options.text: A glass of wine before bed to help the client relax
options.rationale: Alcohol may cause drowsiness but disrupts sleep later in the night.

options.text: Watching television in bed until the client feels drowsy
options.rationale: Television in bed adds light and stimulation; the bed should be kept for sleep.

questions.explanation: Guided imagery, music therapy, and massage are nonpharmacological interventions that promote sleep. Alcohol disrupts sleep later in the night, and watching television in bed works against good sleep hygiene.

questions.prompt: A nurse asks a client who reports poor sleep to keep a sleep diary for 2 weeks. The client asks why. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "It will help us identify your sleep problems and create a plan that fits your lifestyle."
"It's required before you can get a prescription for sleep medication."
"It will show whether you're exaggerating your sleep problems."
"It replaces the need for a sleep study."

questions.explanation: A sleep diary helps the nurse assess the client's sleep habits, identify problems, and collaboratively develop a plan of care tailored to the client's lifestyle, which increases the likelihood the client will follow it.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who is anxious about an upcoming procedure. Which nursing action best promotes the client's comfort?

options.text: Answer the client's questions honestly and allow them to make informed choices about their care.
Tell the client not to worry because everything will be fine.
Limit the information given to avoid increasing the client's anxiety.
Make decisions for the client to reduce their stress.

questions.explanation: Informing clients decreases fear of the unknown. Answering questions honestly and permitting informed choices make clients feel valued, respected, and safe. False reassurance and withholding information are not therapeutic.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reinforcing sleep hygiene teaching with a client who has insomnia. Which instructions should the nurse include? Move the correct instructions to the answer box.

options.text: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, including weekends
options.rationale: A consistent schedule keeps the circadian rhythm steady.

options.text: Keep the bedroom dark, quiet, and cool
options.rationale: A dark, quiet, cool room supports falling and staying asleep.

options.text: Exercise regularly, but not within a few hours of bedtime
options.rationale: Regular exercise improves sleep. Only the timing matters: not right before bed.

options.text: If you can't fall asleep, get up and do something quiet in another room
options.rationale: Lying in bed restless makes it worse. Get up, do something quiet, and come back when tired.

options.text: Watch TV in bed until you feel sleepy
options.rationale: The bed is for sleep and sex only. TV in bed works against sleep.

options.text: Have a cup of coffee after dinner to help you relax
options.rationale: Caffeine should stop 4–6 hours before bed. It's a stimulant, not a relaxant.

options.text: Stay in bed and keep trying until you fall asleep
options.rationale: Staying in bed restless makes insomnia worse. Get up and do something quiet instead.

questions.summary: Same schedule, dark quiet cool room, no caffeine late, bed only for sleep, and exercise that isn't right before bed.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reinforcing teaching with an older adult who takes diphenhydramine to help with sleep. Which adverse effects should the nurse tell the client to watch for? Move the correct effects to the answer box.

options.text: Blurred vision
options.rationale: Anticholinergic effect: can't see.

options.text: Urinary retention
options.rationale: Anticholinergic effect: can't pee.

options.text: Dry mouth
options.rationale: Anticholinergic effect: can't spit.

options.text: Constipation
options.rationale: Anticholinergic effect: can't poop.

options.text: Daytime drowsiness
options.rationale: OTC antihistamine sleep aids often cause next-day drowsiness.

options.text: Diarrhea
options.rationale: Anticholinergics slow the gut, causing constipation, not diarrhea.

options.text: Excess saliva
options.rationale: Anticholinergics dry the mouth. Excess saliva is the opposite effect.

options.text: Frequent urination
options.rationale: Anticholinergics cause urinary retention, not frequent urination.

questions.summary: Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't poop, plus daytime drowsiness.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a class about physical manifestations associated with the fight-or-flight response. Which manifestation should the nurse include?

options.text: Dilated pupils
Decreased blood pressure
Bronchial airway constriction
Hypoglycemia

questions.explanation: Fight-or-flight causes pupil dilation, increased HR, BP, cardiac output, and blood glucose, and bronchial dilation.

questions.prompt: A nurse educator is explaining the HPA axis to a group of nursing students. Which sequence should the educator describe?

options.text: Adrenal glands release ACTH → pituitary releases CRH → hypothalamus releases cortisol
Hypothalamus releases CRH → pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal glands release cortisol
Pituitary releases cortisol → hypothalamus releases ACTH → adrenal glands release CRH
Hypothalamus releases cortisol → adrenal glands release CRH → pituitary releases ACTH

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus releases CRH, which stimulates the pituitary to release ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol.

questions.prompt: A client who has been hospitalized for 2 weeks is irritable, fatigued, and having difficulty concentrating, but vital signs are near their baseline. Which stage of the general adaptation syndrome is the client most likely experiencing?

options.text: Alarm
Resistance
Exhaustion
Countershock

questions.explanation: In the resistance stage, the body resists the stressor and the parasympathetic system moderates fight-or-flight. Fatigue, irritability, and decreased concentration may occur.

questions.prompt: A client who has experienced years of ongoing caregiver stress now has chronic hypertension, depression, and frequent infections. The nurse should recognize these findings as consistent with which of the following?

options.text: The alarm stage
The resistance stage
The exhaustion stage and allostatic load
Allostasis

questions.explanation: In the exhaustion stage, the body's ability to adapt is depleted and prolonged stress leads to illness and allostatic load, the wear and tear that causes conditions like chronic hypertension and depression. Allostasis is the body adjusting to minor stressors.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of students about the general adaptation syndrome. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: The three stages are alarm, resistance, and exhaustion.
options.rationale: GAS moves through alarm, then resistance, then exhaustion.

options.text: It can be triggered by physical or psychological stressors.
options.rationale: Both physical and psychological stressors can start the GAS response.

options.text: Epinephrine release during the exhaustion stage causes the fight-or-flight response.
options.rationale: The fight-or-flight surge of epinephrine happens in the alarm stage.

options.text: It is triggered only by negative events.
options.rationale: GAS occurs with positive and negative stress.

options.text: The exhaustion stage occurs first.
options.rationale: Alarm is the first stage; exhaustion comes last.

questions.explanation: GAS is a three-stage response (alarm, resistance, exhaustion) triggered by physical or psychological stressors, whether positive or negative. Alarm comes first, and epinephrine drives fight or flight in the alarm stage.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a class about sources of stress. The nurse should include that which of the following is an example of a psychological stressor?

options.text: Hypothermia
Financial difficulties
Burn injury
Wrist fracture

questions.explanation: Psychological stressors are events or situations a person interprets as negative or threatening, such as financial difficulties. Hypothermia, burns, and fractures are physiological stressors.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for several clients. Which client is experiencing a physiological stressor?

options.text: A client going through a divorce
A client with severe pain from a hip fracture
A client worried about final exams
A client living in a noisy, crowded apartment

questions.explanation: Physiological stress comes from injury or illness, such as trauma and pain. Divorce and exam pressure are psychological, and a noisy, crowded home is environmental.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing clients' histories for sources of chronic stress. Which findings should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Living in poverty
options.rationale: Poverty is a constant, prolonged stressor.

options.text: Exposure to racism
options.rationale: Ongoing exposure to racism is a source of chronic stress.

options.text: Living with a prolonged illness
options.rationale: A long illness is a constant, prolonged stressor.

options.text: Cramming at the last minute before every exam
options.rationale: Frequent bouts of rushed, short-term stress are episodic acute stress, not chronic stress.

options.text: Being in a minor car accident yesterday
options.rationale: A car accident is a brief, immediate stressor, which is acute stress.

questions.explanation: Chronic stress is constant and prolonged, such as poverty, racism, and prolonged illness. A minor car accident is acute stress, and cramming at the last minute before every exam is episodic acute stress.

questions.prompt: A student tells the school nurse, "I wait until the last minute on every assignment, and I'm always panicking to finish on time." Which type of stress is the student experiencing?

options.text: Traumatic stress
Episodic acute stress
Environmental stress
Physiological stress

questions.explanation: Episodic acute stress is frequent bouts of acute stress, often from taking on too much and feeling rushed and disorganized.

questions.prompt: A family of six lives in a one-bedroom apartment in a neighborhood with frequent violence and no reliable access to food. Which type of stress should the nurse identify?

options.text: Environmental stress
Episodic acute stress
Physiological stress
Traumatic stress

questions.explanation: Environmental stress comes from difficult surroundings such as crowding, housing instability, food insecurity, and neighborhood violence.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about the benefits of exercise for managing stress. Which information should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decreases energy
options.rationale: Regular exercise increases energy rather than draining it.

options.text: Increases mood
options.rationale: Exercise improves mood.

options.text: Inhibits the release of endorphins
options.rationale: Exercise releases endorphins; it does not block them.

options.text: Works for stress only when done at high intensity
options.rationale: Moderate activity also lowers stress; high intensity is not required.

options.text: Improves sleep
options.rationale: Regular exercise improves sleep quality.

questions.explanation: Exercise improves mood and sleep, and it also raises energy, lowers stress, and releases endorphins. Moderate activity is enough to get these benefits.

questions.prompt: Two weeks after being assaulted, a client reports feeling numb and disconnected, is easily startled, and avoids the street where it happened. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Acute stress disorder
Posttraumatic stress disorder
Episodic acute stress
Existential crisis

questions.explanation: ASD starts right after a traumatic event and lasts up to 1 month, with numbness, dissociation, startle, reexperiencing, and avoidance. PTSD is diagnosed if symptoms last beyond 1 month.

questions.prompt: A client who survived a house fire 4 months ago continues to have flashbacks and nightmares about the event. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Acute stress disorder
Posttraumatic stress disorder
Episodic acute stress
Developmental crisis
